title: Radar charts: normalize metrics before comparing profiles
summary: Make each spoke's unit, direction and fixed range explicit; preserve axis order and avoid treating polygon area as a score.
body:
Make each spoke's unit, direction and fixed range explicit; preserve axis order and avoid treating polygon area as a score.

A profile is not a single measure

A radar chart places several ordered metrics on radial spokes and connects one entity's values into a closed profile. It can help a team notice that a delivery operation is strong on timeliness yet weak on geographic coverage. The polygon is a visual index into those separate measurements, not an aggregate score. Before drawing a spoke, state its unit, whether higher or lower is better, and the fixed comparison range. Plotting minutes, percentages and hours on one unnamed radial scale makes the shape meaningless. Use the same definition for every entity and reporting period. A metric called accuracy must retain its denominator and eligibility policy, while a latency metric must say which requests and percentile it covers. Grain and denominator rules, chart questions and dashboard provenance establish those inputs.

Normalize with a documented direction

For each metric, map its declared lower and upper bounds to a common zero-to-one scale. If higher is better, a value at the upper bound maps to one. If lower is better, a value at the lower bound maps to one. The worked contract rejects out-of-range values rather than clipping them without warning. A clipping policy can be useful in an operational dashboard, but a clipped marker must be distinguished from a true value at the boundary. Bounds should come from a versioned target or stable domain rule, not from each panel's current minimum and maximum. Otherwise the same raw value moves when a new peer arrives. Put the raw numbers and their units in the adjacent text table. A normalized 0.8 on delivery time means a position within a declared 15-to-75-minute range; it does not mean 80 percent of deliveries were on time. Axis integrity and bullet targets show the underlying value more directly.

Freeze spoke order and read shape cautiously

The order of spokes changes which values become adjacent and therefore changes the polygon's edges and area, even when the data stay identical. Pick an order by a declared operational grouping or a stable metric schema, then keep it across every panel and export. Repeat the first normalized value only to close the drawing path; do not count that repeated vertex as a sixth metric. A filled polygon can obscure another entity's outline, so compare few entities, label them directly and keep opacity low. Do not rank teams by enclosed area: area is affected by spoke order and radial transformation and has no defensible unit as an overall performance measure. If the goal is exact comparison across eight teams, a grouped dot plot or small multiples usually makes individual differences easier to read. Parallel coordinates handles more profiles, while small multiples avoids overlapping fills.

Make absent and inapplicable metrics visible

A missing accuracy rate should not be drawn at the center, because zero on the normalized axis denotes a measured value at the worst declared bound. Nor should a team with no eligible requests receive an invented score. Show an explicit gap, a separate missing marker, or omit the affected polygon with a reason; keep the metrics table complete. If a spoke is inapplicable to some entities, compare only a documented common metric set or separate those entities into another view. A trend panel should freeze ranges over time, or an apparent improvement can come solely from moving targets. Add text that identifies the largest raw differences and the sample sizes, then let readers inspect each metric separately. Missingness diagnostics, accessible alternatives and export manifests preserve that context.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def prepare_delivery_radar(metric_spec, readings):
    if len(metric_spec) < 3:
        raise ValueError("a radar profile needs at least three spokes")
    metric_names = [name for name, _, _, _ in metric_spec]
    if len(set(metric_names)) != len(metric_names) or set(readings) != set(metric_names):
        raise ValueError("metrics must be unique and match the readings")
    normalized = []
    for name, lower, upper, direction in metric_spec:
        value = readings[name]
        numbers = (lower, upper, value)
        if (not name or direction not in ("higher", "lower") or
                any(isinstance(number, bool) or not isinstance(number, (int, float))
                    or not isfinite(number) for number in numbers) or
                lower >= upper or not lower <= value <= upper):
            raise ValueError(f"invalid range or reading for {name}")
        fraction = (value - lower) / (upper - lower)
        normalized.append(fraction if direction == "higher" else 1 - fraction)
    return metric_names, normalized + normalized[:1]

delivery_metrics = [
    ("delivery_minutes", 15, 75, "lower"),
    ("accuracy_percent", 85, 100, "higher"),
    ("coverage_percent", 60, 100, "higher"),
    ("resolution_hours", 2, 14, "lower"),
]
delivery_readings = {"delivery_minutes": 27, "accuracy_percent": 94,
                     "coverage_percent": 88, "resolution_hours": 5}
spokes, closed_profile = prepare_delivery_radar(delivery_metrics, delivery_readings)
assert spokes == [name for name, _, _, _ in delivery_metrics]
assert [round(value, 2) for value in closed_profile] == [0.8, 0.6, 0.7, 0.75, 0.8]

Performance and operating cost

For K metrics, validation and normalization take O(K) time and O(K) space. Rendering one profile adds K line segments; comparing E profiles adds O(EK) marks and may become unreadable well before computational cost matters. In the worked profile, 27 minutes on a 15-to-75-minute lower-is-better scale maps to 0.8; 94 percent accuracy on an 85-to-100-percent higher-is-better scale maps to 0.6. Coverage maps to 0.7, resolution time to 0.75, and the final 0.8 closes the path. These are four distinct metrics. No mean or area score is implied by the closing coordinate.

Common Mistakes

  • Putting raw minutes, percentages and hours on one radial scale without per-spoke normalization.
  • Recomputing each spoke's bounds from the current comparison group.
  • Treating a polygon's enclosed area as a meaningful total score or ranking.
  • Changing spoke order between entities and then comparing their outlines.
  • Drawing missing or not-applicable metrics at normalized zero without a separate state.

Validation drill

Compare 47 delivery teams on four fixed metrics. Publish each metric's unit, direction, bounds, raw value and eligible population. Show only two profiles at once, keep spoke order fixed, and check the same comparison against a grouped dot plot before asking anyone to rank teams.

title: Waffle charts: allocate whole cells without losing the total
summary: Turn category counts into a fixed grid with an exact denominator, deterministic remainder allocation and labels that preserve small groups.
body:
Turn category counts into a fixed grid with an exact denominator, deterministic remainder allocation and labels that preserve small groups.

A cell is a share, not necessarily a record

A waffle chart represents parts of one whole using a fixed grid of equal-sized cells. A 10-by-10 grid has one hundred visual units; when the underlying cohort contains 83 tickets, one cell represents roughly 0.83 ticket's worth of share, not a literal individual ticket. Say what the whole is and whether every category is mutually exclusive and exhaustive. If the same ticket can be both pending and escalated, it cannot be counted in both cells of a simple part-to-whole grid without an explicit overlap rule. Use a bar chart when precise rank or a small difference matters more than the visual composition. A waffle grid is useful when readers need a quick impression of shares and an adjacent exact-count table is available. Stacked bars, mosaic plots and denominator rules provide useful comparisons.

Allocate a fixed cell budget once

Each category's ideal cell count is its exact count divided by the total, multiplied by the grid size. Independent rounding can produce a grid with 99 or 101 cells. The worked contract first grants each category the floor of its ideal quota, then distributes the remaining cells to the largest fractional remainders. Ties break by the input category order, which is part of the published contract. This guarantees that cell counts sum to the grid size while keeping each allocation near its quota. The categories stay in a stable semantic order rather than sorting by current size on each refresh. If the whole is zero, there is no share to plot; display an empty state instead of a blank grid that could be read as zero in every category. Cumulative categories and scale rules help keep the total visible.

Keep rare groups visible in text

A category below one cell's share may legitimately receive zero colored cells after allocation. Hiding it from the legend would turn a rounding choice into a false claim that the group does not exist. Label every nonzero category with its exact count and percentage, and disclose the cell value. For operational failures, consider a separate rare-case list or a bar chart if one missed record is consequential. More cells improve resolution but make the grid harder to scan on a phone; choose the budget from the question and display size, not from the desire to show every fractional percent. Do not draw a half-filled cell unless its encoding is explained. Multiple waffle charts need the same cell budget, category order and color mapping, and their raw population totals should appear beside each grid. Text alternatives and detail limits protect readers from hidden exceptions.

Make layout and interaction deterministic

A row-major grid fills cells across a row before moving down. A column-major grid produces a different visual boundary; neither changes the counts, but changing the rule between panels can make categories look shifted. Publish rows, columns, fill order and category order. The contract below returns a complete two-dimensional cell ledger so a renderer can color it without recalculating shares. Keyboard or screen-reader output should provide one summary per category instead of announcing one hundred indistinguishable squares. Hovering a cell should describe the category share and exact count, not pretend that a rounded cell corresponds to a particular ticket. When dashboard filters change the cohort, recompute every allocation from the filtered counts and update the denominator in the same transaction. Linked filters, keyboard access and export contracts complete that behavior.

Worked contract

def allocate_ticket_waffle(category_counts, rows: int, columns: int):
    if (not isinstance(rows, int) or isinstance(rows, bool) or rows < 1 or
            not isinstance(columns, int) or isinstance(columns, bool) or columns < 1):
        raise ValueError("grid dimensions must be positive integers")
    if not category_counts:
        raise ValueError("at least one category is required")
    names = [name for name, _ in category_counts]
    if len(set(names)) != len(names) or any(not name for name in names):
        raise ValueError("category names must be unique and nonempty")
    if any(not isinstance(count, int) or isinstance(count, bool) or count < 0
           for _, count in category_counts):
        raise ValueError("counts must be nonnegative integers")
    total = sum(count for _, count in category_counts)
    if total == 0:
        raise ValueError("a zero-size cohort has no shares")
    cell_budget = rows * columns
    floors = [count * cell_budget // total for _, count in category_counts]
    remainders = [count * cell_budget % total for _, count in category_counts]
    extra = cell_budget - sum(floors)
    for index in sorted(range(len(names)), key=lambda index: (-remainders[index], index))[:extra]:
        floors[index] += 1
    grid = [name for name, cells in zip(names, floors) for _ in range(cells)]
    return dict(zip(names, floors)), [grid[offset:offset + columns]
                                      for offset in range(0, cell_budget, columns)]

ticket_counts = [("resolved", 47), ("pending", 29), ("escalated", 7)]
allocation, grid = allocate_ticket_waffle(ticket_counts, rows=10, columns=10)
assert allocation == {"resolved": 57, "pending": 35, "escalated": 8}
assert len(grid) == 10 and all(len(row) == 10 for row in grid)
assert sum(allocation.values()) == 100

Performance and operating cost

For K categories and C cells, exact integer quotas take O(K) time, sorting remainders takes O(K log K), and constructing the cell ledger takes O(C). Space is O(K + C). The sample has 83 tickets: 47 resolved, 29 pending and 7 escalated. In a one-hundred-cell grid, the largest-remainder rule assigns 57, 35 and 8 cells. Those figures total exactly one hundred, but their displayed cell counts are rounded shares of the 83-ticket cohort. The exact counts stay in the legend and export. If the escalated group had fewer than one cell's share, its nonzero count would still need a label even if the allocation gave it no cell.

Common Mistakes

  • Rounding every category independently and drawing a grid with too many or too few cells.
  • Describing each square as one record when the cohort size differs from the cell budget.
  • Dropping a nonzero category from the legend because it received zero rounded cells.
  • Comparing grids with different cell budgets or changing category colors between panels.
  • Counting overlapping categories twice without defining a mutually exclusive partition.

Validation drill

Create two ten-by-ten grids for weekly ticket cohorts of 83 and 47. Reconcile the category counts to each cohort total, allocate cells with one frozen rule, list any nonzero category that receives no cell, and compare the result with a labeled stacked bar.

  • Aggregation grain and denominator: make every plotted mark auditable
  • Accessible charts: encode meaning without relying on color alone

title: Parallel coordinates: make every axis conversion inspectable
summary: Compare multivariate profiles only after documenting normalization, axis order and missing-value treatment.
body:
Compare multivariate profiles only after documenting normalization, axis order and missing-value treatment.

A polyline is one record

Parallel coordinates display one entity as a line crossing several vertical axes. Its crossings are the entity's values; line slopes between axes are visual connectors, not measured rates of change. Before drawing, name every metric and unit. A route whose five service measures have incompatible units cannot be read honestly on one raw height scale. Scale integrity applies independently to every axis. Put the raw value in a tooltip or adjacent table so a normalized line does not erase the original measurement.

Normalization changes the question

Min-max normalization maps each axis to a shared display interval, but a single extreme entity can compress all others. Fixed policy bounds may be more stable than bounds computed from the current filter. If lower is preferable for one metric, invert its display direction and label that inversion. Never silently reverse an axis just to make good records form a tidy line. Target-oriented KPI charts may be clearer if the decision is only whether a threshold was met. Keep the bounds, direction and unit beside each dimension in exported metadata.

Axis order and brushing are analytic choices

Swapping two adjacent axes changes which relationships are visually easiest to see, even though the data stay unchanged. Pick an order tied to the question, such as intake, response, resolution and cost, then preserve it across comparable views. Brushing one range selects entities; a linked table should show which IDs remain and how many were excluded. Linked filters require explicit cohort state. Avoid drawing every record at full opacity: a thousand crossing lines become an opaque band. Sampling must retain a visible selected count and a full-population summary.

Missing values must not become fabricated paths

A line should break or be omitted with an explicit reason when one dimension is absent; zero is not a replacement for missing. Check whether the missingness is related to the outcome being inspected. If only high-cost projects fail to report quality, excluding incomplete records changes the apparent relationship. An export manifest should name complete-case rules, filter state, axis order, bounds and transformed values. For accessibility, offer a sortable table of the underlying records and a concise summary of which dimensions separate selected groups.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def normalize_profile(profile: dict[str, float | None],
                      axes: dict[str, tuple[float, float, bool]]
                      ) -> dict[str, float | None]:
    if set(profile) != set(axes):
        raise ValueError("profile dimensions must match axis declarations")
    normalized = {}
    for metric, (low, high, lower_is_better) in axes.items():
        value = profile[metric]
        if not all(isfinite(bound) for bound in (low, high)) or high <= low:
            raise ValueError("axis bounds must be finite and ordered")
        if value is None:
            normalized[metric] = None
            continue
        if not isfinite(value) or not low <= value <= high:
            raise ValueError("measurement outside declared axis")
        position = (value - low) / (high - low)
        normalized[metric] = 1 - position if lower_is_better else position
    return normalized

axes = {"response_minutes": (0, 120, True),
        "resolved_percent": (0, 100, False)}
depot_profile = normalize_profile(
    {"response_minutes": 47, "resolved_percent": 81}, axes)
assert round(depot_profile["response_minutes"], 4) == 0.6083
assert depot_profile["resolved_percent"] == 0.81

Performance and operating cost

For D dimensions in one record, normalization takes O(D) time and O(D) output space; N records take O(ND). Rendering N polylines can dominate interaction cost, especially when brushing triggers full redraws. The code rejects values outside policy bounds rather than clipping them invisibly. If clipping is intended, export both raw and displayed values and count clipped records by axis.

Common Mistakes

  • Interpreting connector slope as a real-world rate of change.
  • Recomputing axis bounds after a filter and comparing line heights as if scale stayed fixed.
  • Silently reversing one axis or replacing missing with zero.
  • Drawing all records at full opacity and calling the dense band a cluster.

Validation drill

Compare 59 depots on response time, resolution rate and cost. Publish fixed axis bounds, invert only metrics where lower is better, then brush a subgroup and reconcile its ID count to the table.

title: Small multiples: compare groups with honest scales and facet order
summary: Repeat one chart grammar across groups, then choose shared or local axes according to the intended comparison.
body:
Repeat one chart grammar across groups, then choose shared or local axes according to the intended comparison.

A facet is a repeated measurement frame

Small multiples split the same visual grammar into panels, one per group. They reduce line crossings and legend lookup when a single plot has too many series. The gain depends on consistency: each panel should use the same measure, time window, mark type and aggregation rule. A panel for customer tickets and a panel for revenue do not become comparable simply because they share a grid. Declare the measure before arranging panels. Keep a visible label on each panel; color alone is insufficient.

Shared scales answer magnitude questions

If the reader needs to know which depot has the largest delay, a shared y-domain lets equal heights mean equal values. Local y-domains can make a low-volume depot's variation legible, but a steep line then no longer means a larger absolute change. If independent domains are necessary, print the local minimum and maximum in every panel and avoid a headline about cross-panel magnitude. Axis integrity applies to every facet. For percentages, a fixed zero-to-one domain is often an honest baseline; for residuals around zero, a symmetric domain may expose sign and spread better.

Keep the time window and missingness aligned

Shared x-axes help readers distinguish a simultaneous event from a panel-specific shift. A region with no observations on Wednesday should show a gap, not compress its calendar so Thursday occupies Wednesday's position. When groups enter the system at different times, an aligned calendar makes the unequal exposure visible. Time-series gap rules should be applied before faceting. If panels use different time windows by design, label them prominently and avoid visual comparison of positions.

Order panels for the task

Alphabetical order is stable but often unhelpful when inspecting performance. Sorting by a predeclared baseline or current value can put high-risk groups first; automatic resorting on every hover makes the layout hard to track. Record the sort key and freeze it for an analysis session. Do not omit small groups without stating a threshold and the number omitted. Small-sample uncertainty often explains why an apparently extreme panel should receive inspection rather than a confident ranking.

Budget the screen

Thirty tiny panels may be technically complete yet unreadable on a phone. Allow searching or paging through stable groups while keeping the same scale contract. A summary panel can show the total or reference band, but it must follow the same population rules. Test keyboard order and screen-reader panel labels. If each facet needs a unique tooltip, interaction cost grows with the number of panels; prioritize a simple data table for exact values. A chart grid should make comparisons easier, not force the reader to memorize dozens of legends.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def facet_domains(series: dict[str, list[float]],
                  shared: bool) -> dict[str, tuple[float, float]]:
    if not series or any(not values for values in series.values()):
        raise ValueError("each facet needs observed values")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for values in series.values() for value in values):
        raise ValueError("non-finite plotted value")
    if shared:
        values = [value for group in series.values() for value in group]
        domain = (min(values), max(values))
        return {name: domain for name in series}
    return {name: (min(values), max(values)) for name, values in series.items()}

depot_delays = {"north": [18, 47], "south": [3, 8]}
assert facet_domains(depot_delays, True)["south"] == (3, 47)
assert facet_domains(depot_delays, False)["south"] == (3, 8)

Performance and operating cost

For N values across G groups, scanning domains takes O(N + G) time. The shared branch stores an extra O(N) flattened list for clarity; a streaming minimum and maximum reduce that auxiliary memory to O(1), while the returned G domains still need O(G) space. Rendering cost scales with both the number of panels and marks. A UI that rerenders every facet after each filter may become slow even when the domain calculation is cheap; memoize by the complete filter and data-version key only when measurements justify it.

Common Mistakes

  • Using independent y-domains while claiming one group has the larger magnitude.
  • Dropping missing dates and shifting one panel's x positions relative to the rest.
  • Reordering facets during interaction without labeling the sort key.
  • Suppressing tiny cohorts without reporting how many groups were hidden.

Validation drill

Facet five depot delay series on one weekly calendar. Produce a shared-scale view for absolute comparison and a labeled independent-scale view for within-depot variation; write down which conclusions differ.

title: Bullet charts: show a measure, target and performance bands honestly
summary: Keep KPI units and band thresholds explicit instead of compressing context into a gauge.
body:
Keep KPI units and band thresholds explicit instead of compressing context into a gauge.

One axis carries one measure

A bullet chart places an observed value and a target on a shared quantitative scale, often with qualitative background bands. It fits a compact dashboard, but the target and bands must use the same unit and period as the observation. A monthly result against an annual target is not meaningful unless the annual target is allocated by a stated rule. Baseline and axis integrity matter even in a small card. Show the observed number and target in text so the graphic is not the sole carrier of the result.

Treat bands as policy, not decoration

Labels such as below, meets and exceeds imply thresholds selected for a reason. Store the numeric band boundaries and their version. If leadership changes a target, historical cards should either retain the old policy or clearly restate history under the new one. A band extending from 47 to 81 is not an uncertainty interval; it is a classification rule. Uncertainty intervals have a different meaning and should not share the same visual treatment.

Direction changes the interpretation

For revenue, higher may be preferable; for response time, lower may be preferable. The chart's target marker is descriptive until the preferred direction is declared. Put that direction in the accompanying text and label the bands accordingly. A single color progression cannot safely carry this distinction. Accessible text and non-color cues should state whether 68 seconds is better or worse than a target of 59 seconds. A zero target needs a deliberate percentage policy; percent-of-target is undefined there.

Compare cards using a shared contract

Several bullet charts can support comparison only if they use compatible axes or clearly named units. Autoscaling each card to its own maximum makes equal lengths represent different values. If metrics use incompatible units, separate panels and display target-relative gaps explicitly, rather than placing them on one fake common scale. Signed gap views may be clearer for ranking departures from target. Export raw value, target, bands, direction and period. Check missing observations and partial periods before applying a performance label.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def classify_kpi(observed: float, target: float,
                 minimum: float, maximum: float,
                 lower_is_better: bool) -> tuple[float, str]:
    values = (observed, target, minimum, maximum)
    if any(not isfinite(value) for value in values):
        raise ValueError("KPI values must be finite")
    if not minimum <= observed <= maximum or not minimum <= target <= maximum:
        raise ValueError("measure or target outside axis")
    gap = observed - target
    meets = observed <= target if lower_is_better else observed >= target
    return gap, "meets target" if meets else "misses target"

response_kpi = classify_kpi(68, 59, 0, 120, lower_is_better=True)
assert response_kpi == (9, "misses target")
revenue_kpi = classify_kpi(81, 59, 0, 120, lower_is_better=False)
assert revenue_kpi == (22, "meets target")

Performance and operating cost

Classifying one card takes O(1) time and space; N cards take O(N). Rendering cost is small, but target lookup and policy versioning dominate operational correctness. The code checks a shared axis and preferred direction. It does not invent background bands or calculate a percentage when the target is zero. Store band thresholds and time period with the emitted card to make historical comparisons reproducible.

Common Mistakes

  • Comparing a monthly observed value with an annual target.
  • Using attractive background bands without a stated threshold policy.
  • Assuming higher is always better.
  • Letting each card auto-scale while comparing bar lengths across cards.

Validation drill

Build three service KPI cards: response time, resolved tickets and refund rate. Declare direction, target, axis and band policy for each, then test a missing observation and a zero target.

title: Dashboard filters and provenance: make every view reproducible
summary: A dashboard is a family of data queries; each control changes the population and needs an explicit, inspectable state.
body:
A dashboard is a family of data queries; each control changes the population and needs an explicit, inspectable state.

Version the query state

A screenshot of a 74 percent review rate means little without period, channel, eligibility version and data-refresh time. Encode those fields in a shareable state record. If a filter changes the cohort, recompute counts and intervals rather than carrying cached percentages across populations. The denominator must travel with every filtered value.

Manage defaults

A default “last 30 days” view moves each day. Use a fixed reporting cutoff for reproducible review packets and mark live periods provisional. If the dashboard initially excludes low-volume channels, disclose that exclusion rather than implying the total includes all channels. Make “all eligible channels” a testable state.

Prevent stale joins

A filter change may return fast chart data while the companion table or alternative text still shows the previous request. Apply response IDs or cancellation to keep all representations synchronized. The data pipeline should expose snapshot ID and query version. Publication boundaries offer a model for replacing a complete snapshot atomically.

Reproduce a decision

Save a review packet with filter state, metric definition, source snapshot, numerator, denominator and chart version. Re-run it after a late receipt arrives; the old packet must remain explainable even if the live dashboard changes. Test an invalid channel and a period with no eligible receipts rather than silently falling back to another state.

Implementation

def dashboard_state(snapshot_id, start_day, end_day, channels):
    if not snapshot_id or start_day >= end_day:
        raise ValueError("invalid snapshot or period")
    selected = tuple(sorted(set(channels)))
    if not selected:
        raise ValueError("select at least one channel")
    return {"snapshot_id": snapshot_id, "start_day": start_day,
            "end_day": end_day, "channels": selected}

Performance and operating cost

Canonicalizing C selected channels costs O(C log C) time and O(C) space. Query and render costs depend on the backend and mark count; a versioned aggregate cache can help, but its key must include every population-changing filter.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not publish a decision screenshot without snapshot and filter state.
  • Do not reuse an overall interval after changing the cohort.
  • Do not let chart, table and alternative text resolve different query responses.

title: Stacked bars: separate composition from volume and preserve denominators
summary: Use absolute and normalized stacks for different questions, and retain every segment count.
body:
Use absolute and normalized stacks for different questions, and retain every segment count.

A stack has two possible questions

An absolute stacked bar shows a total and its parts in the same unit. A normalized bar forces every total to one and shows the mix instead. These are not interchangeable. If depot A closes 47 of 81 requests while depot B closes 470 of 810, both have the same closed share, but the latter carries ten times the workload. Place total and share in adjacent views when both matter. Define the denominator before calculating either bar. The title should say whether the horizontal extent means requests or a fraction of eligible requests.

Keep categories stable

Assign each status one color and one position across periods. If a status disappears, retain its zero-valued place in the data contract rather than shifting every later segment. The unanchored middle segments in a stack are difficult to compare precisely; when one category is the focus, use a grouped bar or a separate trend. Sort bars by a declared metric, such as eligible volume, and keep that order fixed across comparison panels. Facet ordering follows the same rule.

Handle absent and ineligible records

A missing status is not necessarily a measured zero. If the warehouse omits unresolved requests, a normalized stack can show an apparently perfect closure rate even as the unobserved group grows. Reconcile segment counts to the cohort total, expose an unknown state, and reserve a separate no-exposure state when the denominator is zero. A percentage bar for zero eligible requests has no defined composition. Missing-state display should use a label or pattern in addition to color.

Audit every filter

When a dashboard filters by region or week, recompute each segment count from the selected cohort and normalize only after filtering. Do not average prior percentages. Tooltips and exports should include segment count, denominator and percentage; rounded shares may sum to 99.9 or 100.1, which is a display effect rather than a data error. Linked selections must update totals and segments together. Test one-bar, zero-cohort and category-absent states before release.

Worked contract

def composition_by_depot(
    counts: dict[str, dict[str, int]], statuses: tuple[str, ...]
) -> dict[str, dict[str, tuple[int, float | None]]]:
    if len(set(statuses)) != len(statuses) or not statuses:
        raise ValueError("statuses must be unique and nonempty")
    result = {}
    for depot, segments in counts.items():
        if set(segments) - set(statuses) or any(value < 0 for value in segments.values()):
            raise ValueError("unknown status or negative count")
        total = sum(segments.values())
        result[depot] = {
            status: (segments.get(status, 0),
                     segments.get(status, 0) / total if total else None)
            for status in statuses
        }
    return result

mix = composition_by_depot(
    {"north": {"closed": 47, "pending": 34},
     "south": {"closed": 470, "pending": 340}},
    ("closed", "pending", "unknown"))
assert mix["north"]["closed"] == (47, 47 / 81)
assert mix["south"]["closed"] == (470, 470 / 810)
assert mix["north"]["unknown"] == (0, 0.0)

Performance and operating cost

For D depots, S declared statuses and M supplied segment values, validation and construction take O(M + DS) expected time and O(DS) output space. Reusing a prebuilt status set removes repeated set construction in a larger implementation. Rendering a normalized bar still needs the absolute counts for labels and audit. The example treats an absent segment as observed zero only under the stated complete-status contract; without that contract, an absent segment must be marked unknown.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading equal-width normalized bars as equal workloads.
  • Dropping unresolved statuses before calculating shares.
  • Changing stack order between weeks and implying a category moved.
  • Averaging percentages instead of adding segment counts first.

Validation drill

Prepare 13 weekly depot bars with different cohort sizes. Show absolute and normalized versions, then remove one status record from a source extract and verify reconciliation fails rather than silently improving a percentage.

title: Mosaic plots: make cell area match the underlying count
summary: Use widths and conditional heights to expose how two categorical variables share one total.
body:
Use widths and conditional heights to expose how two categorical variables share one total.

Choose a denominator before drawing tiles

A two-way mosaic plot partitions one rectangle by a contingency table. Each first-category column gets width proportional to its count in the full data set. Within that column, second-category tile heights represent conditional shares. Multiplying width by height yields the cell's share of the grand total. That area contract is the point of the chart. If the column widths are all equal instead, the display answers a different question: it emphasizes within-group composition and conceals unequal group sizes. Stacked bars are often easier to read when exact conditional rates are the primary comparison, while treemaps use area for hierarchical totals rather than a two-way cross-classification.

Declare the table grain

Count one unit only once in the table unless the chart explicitly represents events rather than entities. If a shipment can appear in several outcome categories, a standard contingency table is not valid until a mutually exclusive rule is chosen. A missing outcome is its own category or an explicit exclusion; quietly dropping it changes every tile's area. Aggregation grain and denominator should be fixed upstream. Record the category order even if one group has a zero count, and distinguish a true zero cell from a category never collected. Reconcile each column subtotal with source records before calculating widths, then reconcile all columns to the grand total. A plot that looks rectangular can still be numerically wrong.

Read association without mistaking size for rate

A wider group contributes more observations, while a taller tile within that group represents a larger conditional share. Readers often compare tile heights across groups and forget the width, or compare areas when the question is only about rates. Label both count and within-group percentage in a companion table. If a tiny tile cannot hold text, put the label outside or leave it to an accessible table rather than enlarging the tile. Heatmaps can encode a rate in color, but their equal-size cells do not show count automatically. Do not imply statistical significance from a striking mosaic pattern; sampling design, uncertainty and multiple subgroup inspections remain separate questions.

Keep order and coverage stable

A mosaic is more legible with a limited number of well-defined categories. Many thin columns or slivers make the visual fragile on phones and at high zoom. Sort categories by a declared business order, not by whichever tile creates the strongest pattern in each filter state. If a dashboard filter removes units, recompute column totals and display the new grand total; a stale denominator can make area and labels disagree. Linked filters should expose which cohort is selected. Export the exact cross-tabulation with count, row total, grand total, conditional percentage and excluded count so the visible geometry can be independently reconstructed.

Worked contract

def mosaic_tiles(table: dict[str, dict[str, int]],
                 outcomes: list[str]):
    if not table or not outcomes or len(outcomes) != len(set(outcomes)):
        raise ValueError("groups and ordered outcomes are required")
    if any(set(cells) != set(outcomes) for cells in table.values()):
        raise ValueError("every group needs every outcome, including zeros")
    if any(type(count) is not int or count < 0
           for cells in table.values() for count in cells.values()):
        raise ValueError("counts must be nonnegative integers")
    group_totals = {group: sum(cells.values()) for group, cells in table.items()}
    if any(total == 0 for total in group_totals.values()):
        raise ValueError("empty groups need a separate missing-data state")
    grand_total = sum(group_totals.values())
    tiles, left = [], 0.0
    for group, cells in table.items():
        right = left + group_totals[group] / grand_total
        bottom = 0.0
        for outcome in outcomes:
            top = bottom + cells[outcome] / group_totals[group]
            tiles.append((group, outcome, left, right, bottom, top,
                          cells[outcome]))
            bottom = top
        left = right
    return tiles

review_counts = {
    "early shift": {"accepted": 47, "returned": 13},
    "late shift": {"accepted": 20, "returned": 20},
}
review_tiles = mosaic_tiles(review_counts, ["accepted", "returned"])
early_accepted = review_tiles[0]
assert abs((early_accepted[3] - early_accepted[2]) *
           (early_accepted[5] - early_accepted[4]) - 0.47) < 1e-12
assert review_tiles[-1][-1] == 20

Performance and operating cost

For G groups and K outcome categories, validation and tile construction take O(GK) time and O(GK) output space. The positions are normalized to a unit square; the first tile covers 47 percent of the area because 47 of 100 reviewed shipments fall in that cell. Floating-point boundaries are drawing coordinates, not replacement counts. Keep the integer table available for labels and audit exports.

Common Mistakes

  • Making every group equally wide while claiming tile area represents total count.
  • Dropping unknown outcomes without updating the denominator and exclusion note.
  • Enlarging tiny tiles to fit labels, which breaks the area contract.
  • Reading an attractive pattern as evidence of association without examining uncertainty or sampling.

Validation drill

Cross-tabulate 83 inspected shipments by shift and disposition, including an unknown disposition. Reconcile the grand total and verify that each tile area equals its cell count divided by 83.

title: Aggregation grain and denominator: make every plotted mark auditable
summary: A visual aggregate is trustworthy only when each source row, grouping key and denominator have a declared meaning.
body:
A visual aggregate is trustworthy only when each source row, grouping key and denominator have a declared meaning.

Fix the source grain

A receipt table can contain one row per receipt while a status log contains several rows per receipt. Joining them and counting rows creates a review volume that rises when the workflow emits more events. Reduce the log to one terminal outcome per receipt before joining, or build an explicit event-level chart. Join cardinality is a precondition for visual accuracy.

Choose the denominator

A chart titled “review completion rate” needs a rule for receipts that were submitted but not yet eligible, rejected at intake or still open. Keep numerator and denominator alongside the plotted rate in the data contract. When filtering by channel, recompute both counts for the filtered cohort; never filter precomputed overall rates and average them.

Control time bins

A daily chart needs one time zone, one interval convention and an explicit policy for late events. A receipt submitted at 23:58 and completed after midnight might belong to the submission-day cohort even though its completion event occurs next day. Calendar policy keeps those two clocks apart. Document whether incomplete days are omitted or shown as provisional.

Reconcile the visual

For two channels with 34 of 47 and 18 of 23 timely receipts, the combined rate is 52 of 70, about 74.3 percent. The simple average of the two channel percentages is different. Test that the dashboard total uses summed counts. Include an empty group and one duplicated receipt ID to catch silent inflation.

Implementation

def weighted_completion_rate(channel_counts):
    timely = 0
    eligible = 0
    for timely_count, eligible_count in channel_counts:
        if not 0 <= timely_count <= eligible_count:
            raise ValueError("invalid channel counts")
        timely += timely_count
        eligible += eligible_count
    return None if eligible == 0 else timely / eligible

Performance and operating cost

Aggregating N rows by C keys is O(N) expected time and O(C) state with a hash map. Sorting labels adds O(C log C). A database group-by can move the work closer to the source, but its join and filter contracts still need inspection.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not average percentages when group sizes differ.
  • Do not count event rows as independent receipts.
  • Do not combine submission and completion timestamps without a cohort rule.

title: Interactive dashboards: recompute cohorts after linked filters
summary: Make selections compose predictably, recalculate numerators and denominators, and expose the active state.
body:
Make selections compose predictably, recalculate numerators and denominators, and expose the active state.

A selection changes the population

Linked filtering lets a selection in one view constrain another. Clicking a depot, brushing a date range or choosing a channel changes the cohort behind every plotted metric. The interaction contract must specify whether filters combine with AND or OR, whether a second click toggles, and whether an empty selection means all or none. Show active filters in text and offer a clear reset. Dashboard provenance needs the same filter state that the user sees; otherwise a shared screenshot cannot be reproduced.

Recompute base counts

A precomputed overall completion percentage cannot simply be filtered and averaged. Reapply the filter to eligible records, then sum timely and eligible counts for the selected cohort. If a record appears in both a status log and an order table, deduplicate to the declared unit before counting. Grain and denominator rules are the invariant under interaction. A filtered group with zero eligible records should display an undefined rate and zero denominator, not a zero-percent success rate.

Synchronize every view

When a brush narrows a chart, its companion count, data table, map and export must use the same selected IDs or query predicate. Some dashboards filter the marks but leave the headline KPI unfiltered; users then compare incompatible populations. Carry one normalized state object and one data-version token into each query. If a backend response arrives after the user changes filters again, discard the stale response instead of replacing a newer view. A request ID or abort signal can enforce this. Large-series rendering may be approximate, but filter semantics must remain exact.

Make selection discoverable and reversible

Hover-only behavior hides controls from touch and keyboard users. Provide visible filter chips, keyboard-operable controls, focus cues and a readable selection summary. Color should not be the sole indication of selected marks. A reset should restore the documented default and preserve the date or snapshot policy, not silently switch to today's data. Accessible chart controls include data values outside the plotted canvas. Keep the browser back button or a shareable query state when deep analysis paths matter.

Test the state machine

Exercise no filters, one filter, two intersecting filters, mutually exclusive filters, a zero-eligible result, and rapid filter changes. Compare chart, KPI and export row counts for each state. For a selected region and channel, check that removing one chip broadens the cohort only along that dimension. Record the expected query predicate alongside a screenshot in a release test. If the chart is based on sampled or aggregated data, do not use a pixel brush to imply record-level exactness unless the backend can resolve it.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ReviewRecord:
    receipt_id: str
    region: str
    channel: str
    eligible: bool
    timely: bool

def filtered_completion(records: list[ReviewRecord],
                        regions: set[str], channels: set[str]
                        ) -> tuple[int, int, float | None]:
    if len({record.receipt_id for record in records}) != len(records):
        raise ValueError("duplicate receipt identity")
    selected = [record for record in records
                if (not regions or record.region in regions)
                and (not channels or record.channel in channels)
                and record.eligible]
    if any(record.timely and not record.eligible for record in records):
        raise ValueError("timely receipt cannot be ineligible")
    timely = sum(record.timely for record in selected)
    eligible = len(selected)
    return timely, eligible, timely / eligible if eligible else None

receipts = [ReviewRecord("r-47", "north", "web", True, True),
            ReviewRecord("r-81", "north", "store", True, False),
            ReviewRecord("r-94", "south", "web", True, True)]
assert filtered_completion(receipts, {"north"}, {"web"}) == (1, 1, 1.0)
assert filtered_completion(receipts, {"south"}, {"store"}) == (0, 0, None)

Performance and operating cost

For N records, duplicate validation and filtering take O(N) expected time and O(N) temporary space in this direct version; the selected list can be avoided with streaming counters to use O(N) identity state and O(1) additional cohort state. For a remote dashboard, query cost and transfer volume usually dominate. Cache only by normalized filters, authorization context and data version. Never reuse a cached result across tenants or revisions merely because the visible filter chips match.

Common Mistakes

  • Filtering colored marks while leaving headline metrics on the full population.
  • Averaging cached percentages after a filter instead of summing base counts.
  • Treating an empty cohort as a measured zero-percent rate.
  • Letting an older network response overwrite the result of a newer selection.

Validation drill

Connect a weekly trend, region bar chart and completion KPI. Test six filter states and verify the same eligible count in the chart tooltip, KPI, table and CSV export for each state.

title: Chart design starts with a question, unit and visual encoding
summary: A chart is a visual comparison over defined observations; its marks and axes must preserve the quantity the reader is meant to compare.
body:
A chart is a visual comparison over defined observations; its marks and axes must preserve the quantity the reader is meant to compare.

Write the comparison

A receipt operations report might ask whether the share of reviews completed within 24 hours changed by channel. That is a rate by category and period, not a count of tickets. Record the population, numerator, denominator, time window and update cadence before picking a shape. Metric denominators belong in the chart contract because a change in eligibility can look like a change in performance.

Map quantities to marks

Position on a common scale is useful for comparing rates across channels; a bar chart makes zero a visible reference. Use a line only when adjacent points are connected by an ordered process such as time. A scatter plot asks whether two numeric quantities move together. A decorative shape must not imply a numerical relationship the dataset does not contain.

Preserve context

Show units, sample counts and the period cutoff. A rate can rise when a low-volume channel disappears even if no channel improves. Add a small companion table or labels with denominators when that composition matters. Aggregation grain determines what the visual mark actually represents. Never use a legend to hide a definition required to read the chart.

Specify a review fixture

Create one channel with 34 timely reviews out of 47 receipts and another with 18 out of 23. The second bar is higher despite its lower count. Ask a reviewer to state that distinction from the figure alone, then test an empty channel. Empty is missing evidence, not a zero percent service rate.

Implementation

def channel_completion_rate(timely_count, eligible_count):
    if eligible_count < 0 or timely_count < 0 or timely_count > eligible_count:
        raise ValueError("invalid receipt counts")
    return None if eligible_count == 0 else timely_count / eligible_count

channel_rates = {
    "portal": channel_completion_rate(34, 47),
    "email": channel_completion_rate(18, 23),
}

Performance and operating cost

Computing C channel rates is O(C) time and O(C) output space. Rendering cost grows with the number of marks, labels and interaction states; filter or aggregate only under a stated rule so the viewer can recover the denominator.

  • Do not substitute counts for rates when channel volumes differ.
  • Do not connect unordered categories with a line.
  • Do not render an empty denominator as a measured zero.

title: Axis scales, baselines and labels: prevent a correct number from telling a false story
summary: Axis choices change visual distance, so the scale must match the comparison and be disclosed wherever it changes interpretation.
body:
Axis choices change visual distance, so the scale must match the comparison and be disclosed wherever it changes interpretation.

Use a meaningful baseline

Bar length is read against its baseline. Starting a bar axis at 0.71 can make two completion rates of 0.74 and 0.77 look several times apart. Use zero for ordinary bar lengths and show exact values when a small difference matters. A line chart may use a narrower range to show variation, but the displayed bounds and units must remain obvious.

Inspect transformations

A logarithmic axis can reveal values across orders of magnitude, but equal screen distances then represent equal ratios rather than equal differences. Zero and negative values need an explicit treatment. Never switch an axis to logarithmic merely to fit an outlier, and never compare a linear-panel slope with a log-panel slope as though they share meaning.

Keep category order honest

Sort categories by a documented metric or a stable domain order. If the order changes at each refresh, motion can look like a performance shift when values are steady. Labels should state percent versus percentage points; moving from 74 to 77 percent is a three-point change, not a three-percent relative change. The chart question decides which comparison is primary.

Test presentation rules

Prepare two rates, 0.74 and 0.77, and verify both bars share zero. Then format them as 74.0% and 77.0%. If a narrow view clips labels, retain an accessible text table. Recheck after filtering because an automatic axis may silently rescale and change the apparent difference.

Implementation

def percentage_point_change(previous_rate, current_rate):
    if not all(0 <= rate <= 1 for rate in (previous_rate, current_rate)):
        raise ValueError("rates must be between zero and one")
    return (current_rate - previous_rate) * 100

change_points = percentage_point_change(0.74, 0.77)

Performance and operating cost

Scale formatting is O(M) for M plotted marks. The larger cost is review: test every filter state that changes axis bounds, zero visibility or label collisions. Cache formatted labels only when underlying rate and unit versions match.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not truncate a bar axis without making the baseline explicit.
  • Do not label a percentage-point movement as a relative percent.
  • Do not hide nonpositive observations when using a logarithmic scale.

title: Distribution plots: keep the tail, missing values and bin policy visible
summary: Histograms and quantile summaries answer shape questions that a single mean or trend line cannot settle.
body:
Histograms and quantile summaries answer shape questions that a single mean or trend line cannot settle.

Distinguish populations

Review delay among completed receipts excludes receipts still open. A histogram of completed delays therefore cannot describe the full submission cohort without a censoring policy. State the population and cutoff. Distribution summaries help reveal a long tail, while a separate pending count shows records that do not yet have a delay.

Choose bins deliberately

A histogram with bins of one hour may appear noisy; a bin of one day can conceal a 24-hour service threshold. Fix bin edges across compared periods and label whether the left or right edge is included. Do not auto-bin each channel independently and then compare the resulting bar heights as though the units were identical.

Retain the tail

A rare 47-hour delay can matter more operationally than a high-volume cluster near five hours. If the axis is cropped to show the center, disclose the number above the cap and provide a full-range or quantile companion view. Invalid negative delays should be separated from valid extremes. Axis policy must remain stable across cohorts.

Make a small fixture

Start with delays of 3, 4, 5, 6 and 47 hours. The mean is 13 and the median is 5. A chart that omits the last value while still reporting the original mean is internally inconsistent. Test zero valid observations, one extreme observation and a delayed arrival that changes a closed reporting period.

Implementation

def delay_bins(delays_hours, edges):
    if len(edges) < 2 or edges[0] < 0 or any(left >= right for left, right in zip(edges, edges[1:])):
        raise ValueError("bin edges must increase from a nonnegative start")
    counts = [0] * (len(edges) - 1)
    overflow = 0
    for delay in delays_hours:
        if delay < edges[0]:
            raise ValueError("delay falls below the declared range")
        location = next((index for index, (left, right) in enumerate(zip(edges, edges[1:]))
                         if left <= delay < right), None)
        if location is None:
            overflow += 1
        else:
            counts[location] += 1
    return counts, overflow

Performance and operating cost

This direct bin search costs O(NB) for N observations and B bins, with O(B) output space. A binary search on sorted edges reduces lookup to O(N log B). Store missing and overflow counts separately so a faster renderer cannot erase them.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not compare histograms with different bin edges as if they were identical.
  • Do not trim a valid operational tail without reporting the omitted count.
  • Do not treat an unfinished receipt as a completed zero-hour delay.

title: Uncertainty on charts: show denominators and intervals beside estimates
summary: A plotted estimate is not a population fact; its uncertainty and sample unit affect how strongly a visual difference can be read.
body:
A plotted estimate is not a population fact; its uncertainty and sample unit affect how strongly a visual difference can be read.

Show the independent count

Two channels can both report a 75 percent completion rate, yet one may have 12 receipts and another 12,000. Put eligible counts near marks or in an accessible companion table. If customers submit repeated receipts, the independent count may be customers rather than rows. Cluster resampling keeps those observations together.

Choose an interval contract

Specify the estimator, interval construction, confidence level and sampling unit. Error bars from an independent-row formula are misleading when assignments or outcomes cluster by reviewer. A confidence interval describes a repeated-sampling procedure; it is not a probability distribution over the displayed fixed rate. Coverage requires a valid observation process.

Separate overlap from decision

Overlapping intervals do not by themselves establish that a difference is absent, and nonoverlap is not a universal experiment test. If the task is to compare channels, calculate and display an interval for the difference under the study design. Pair this with practical limits: a two-point change may matter only above a declared volume or cost threshold.

Handle thin groups

A filter may leave one receipt or none. Use a visible “insufficient data” state rather than a narrow-looking point with absent error bars. Check that each interval is within the metric domain and that chart tooling does not clip it without notice. Keep the raw numerator and denominator available for audit.

Implementation

def interval_mark(point_rate, lower_rate, upper_rate, eligible_count):
    if eligible_count < 2:
        return {"state": "insufficient_data", "eligible_count": eligible_count}
    if not 0 <= lower_rate <= point_rate <= upper_rate <= 1:
        raise ValueError("invalid rate interval")
    return {"state": "measured", "point": point_rate,
            "lower": lower_rate, "upper": upper_rate, "eligible_count": eligible_count}

Performance and operating cost

Formatting M intervals is O(M) time and space. Interval estimation may be much more expensive, especially when resampling clusters; calculate it in a versioned data job and render the stored estimate with its construction metadata.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not draw error bars without naming their meaning.
  • Do not use receipt count as the independent sample size when customers repeat.
  • Do not interpret overlapping intervals as a complete test of a difference.

title: Accessible charts: encode meaning without relying on color alone
summary: A chart needs legible labels, keyboard access where interactive, and a text route to the same substantive data.
body:
A chart needs legible labels, keyboard access where interactive, and a text route to the same substantive data.

Keep meaning redundant

A red and green pair is not enough to distinguish two completion series. Use direct labels, distinct line styles or marker shapes, and a legend that names the measured groups. Color can reinforce meaning but should not carry it alone. Axis labels must include units and remain legible at narrow widths.

Write a useful alternative

An image alternative should state the main comparison and notable exception, not simply “bar chart.” A companion table should expose exact values, periods and denominators for readers who cannot use the graphic. For an interactive chart, its filter controls need visible names, keyboard focus and a text update when the dataset changes.

Test the states

Check high zoom, narrow layout, monochrome output and keyboard-only interaction. A hover tooltip is not an adequate source of the only exact value. If a tooltip reports 74 percent but the accessible table says 73.6 percent, declare rounding once and use it consistently. Dashboard filters must update both representations together.

Budget complexity

A dense chart with 40 small labels may be technically accessible but still hard to scan. Reduce visible series, use a stable sort and provide a drill-down or table for detail. Retain disclosure of hidden groups and totals so simplification does not selectively remove an unfavorable channel.

Implementation

def chart_alt_text(period_label, channel_rates):
    measured = [(channel, rate) for channel, rate in channel_rates.items() if rate is not None]
    if not measured:
        return f"{period_label}: no channel has an eligible denominator."
    highest_channel, highest_rate = max(measured, key=lambda item: item[1])
    return (f"{period_label}: {len(measured)} channels measured; "
            f"{highest_channel} has the highest completion rate at {highest_rate:.1%}.")

Performance and operating cost

A short alternative over C channels costs O(C) time and O(C) temporary space in this implementation. For larger datasets, aggregate once and reuse the exact result for chart, table and alternative text to prevent divergence.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not rely on hue alone to identify a series.
  • Do not put the only exact value in a pointer-only tooltip.
  • Do not write alternative text from stale data after filters change.

title: Time-series charts: distinguish missing days, zeros and provisional periods
summary: Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.
body:
Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.

A line implies continuity

A time-series chart maps measurements to ordered instants or calendar periods. Connecting two observed points across an unobserved day implies a path that was never measured. A recorded zero is different: it says the instrument or process observed the period and counted none. Store both the period key and an observation-status field before drawing the line. The observation calendar defines which periods were expected. Use a visible break, hollow mark, or separate missingness strip when a period has no measurement; do not silently replace it with zero.

Name the two clocks

Operational data often has an event timestamp and a processing timestamp. A refund received late may belong to Tuesday's customer cohort but be visible only on Thursday's dashboard. Choose the clock that answers the chart's question and label it in the axis or subtitle. When bucketing timestamps into local days, choose one time zone and convert before taking the date. Daylight-saving changes make a local day shorter or longer than 24 hours in some regions. An elapsed-duration chart should use instants; a calendar-day chart should use dates in the declared zone.

Mark provisional periods

A current day is incomplete even when its count is known so far. Drawing it with the same line and scale as closed days invites a false decline. Carry a finalized flag from the data source, and either exclude the open interval or render it with a different stroke and an explicit as-of time. Late corrections can reopen an earlier point, so the chart's data-version label matters. A reader must know whether yesterday is final, not only whether the plotting job ran.

Protect the comparison

Never join lines across a product outage, a changed population, or a denominator change without an annotation or split. Keep the y-axis unit and calculation stable across the displayed range. If one week contains 42, 47 and 51 eligible cases while the next has a different intake rule, raw counts compare different populations. The aggregation contract should produce both numerator and denominator where a rate is intended. A moving average may reduce noise, but its window, edge behavior and missing-day policy must be stated.

Check the drawn output

Test an interior missing day, an observed zero, an incomplete final day, a late revision, and a daylight-saving boundary for the region being displayed. Confirm that hover text, downloadable data and the axis all use the same period key. A chart-library setting that connects nulls can undo a carefully prepared missingness contract. Inspect the rendered image, not only the input array. The text alternative should report the gap and the as-of timestamp too.

Worked contract

from datetime import date, timedelta

def complete_daily_series(observed: dict[date, int],
                          start: date, end: date) -> list[tuple[date, int | None]]:
    if end < start or any(count < 0 for count in observed.values()):
        raise ValueError("invalid date range or count")
    if any(day < start or day > end for day in observed):
        raise ValueError("observation outside display range")
    return [(start + timedelta(days=offset),
             observed.get(start + timedelta(days=offset)))
            for offset in range((end - start).days + 1)]

points = complete_daily_series(
    {date(2026, 8, 11): 47, date(2026, 8, 13): 0},
    date(2026, 8, 11), date(2026, 8, 13))
assert [count for _, count in points] == [47, None, 0]

Performance and operating cost

For D expected periods and O observed keys, validation plus calendar completion takes O(D + O) time and O(D) output space. The code assumes an already chosen calendar zone and one authoritative count per day. Converting event timestamps and resolving duplicates belong upstream. For a long history, query only the visible interval, and keep finalization state beside each point; creating a million empty periods in a browser is a serving error, not a charting technique.

Common Mistakes

  • Converting an unobserved period into zero and drawing a continuous line.
  • Bucketing by server time zone while labeling the axis with the user's local dates.
  • Treating today's partial count as a completed daily value.
  • Using a rolling average without showing its window and missing-period rule.

title: Dense scatterplots: reveal overlap without hiding rare observations
summary: Use density cells and deliberate sampling when points overlap, while retaining the populations and exceptions that matter.
body:
Use density cells and deliberate sampling when points overlap, while retaining the populations and exceptions that matter.

Overplotting changes what a point means

A scatterplot maps paired values to two position channels. When thousands of records land on the same pixels, the visible mark count no longer approximates the record count. Transparency can expose a dense center, but repeated strokes saturate and rare points can disappear beneath it. Before changing the mark style, count records per screen-space cell and inspect whether the question is about density, outliers, groups or exact cases. The chart question determines whether a point cloud is still the right view.

Bin at a declared resolution

A two-dimensional density grid counts observations inside fixed x and y intervals. It can show population structure without rendering every dot. The cells need axis units, bounds and bin width; changing cell size changes the picture. A cell count is not a probability unless divided by the declared population or area. Use the same grid for comparisons across cohorts, otherwise apparent hot spots may be a change in binning. Preserve a drill-down path to the original records where access rules permit it. A heatmap of density has the same color-domain obligations as any other heatmap.

Sampling is a data product

Uniform sampling can make a common cluster readable yet omit a rare but important failure mode. If the operational question concerns unusual refunds, retain those cases deliberately and label the sample design. A stratified sample can hold a fixed number from each category, but its plotted mix no longer reflects population proportions unless weights or counts are shown. Never present sampled points as the full dataset. Record the random seed, inclusion rule and population size. The sampling frame matters even when the result is only exploratory.

Separate trend from uncertainty

A diagonal cloud does not by itself establish a causal effect. Outliers, groups and repeated measures can alter the apparent slope. Show marginal distributions or group facets when one cluster masks another. If a fitted trend is added, distinguish raw marks from the fitted line and state whether the fit is weighted, filtered or calculated on the visible sample. Influence checks are needed before treating that line as a stable summary. A truncated axis can also make a weak relation seem strong.

Validate at the pixel budget

Test identical coordinates, boundary points, non-finite values and a small rare cohort. Count how many records end in each visible density cell, then reconcile the total with the filtered input. Hovering a cell should report its count and ranges, not invent a single representative record. At high density, compare a grid and a sampled-point layer side by side: the grid describes mass, while the points retain individual exceptions. On a small screen, favor one readable layer over simultaneous translucent layers that obscure both.

Worked contract

from math import floor, isfinite

def density_cells(points: list[tuple[float, float]],
                  x_bounds: tuple[float, float],
                  y_bounds: tuple[float, float],
                  columns: int, rows: int) -> dict[tuple[int, int], int]:
    x_low, x_high = x_bounds
    y_low, y_high = y_bounds
    if columns < 1 or rows < 1 or x_low >= x_high or y_low >= y_high:
        raise ValueError("invalid grid")
    counts: dict[tuple[int, int], int] = {}
    for amount, handling_minutes in points:
        if not all(map(isfinite, (amount, handling_minutes))):
            raise ValueError("non-finite observation")
        if not (x_low <= amount <= x_high and
                y_low <= handling_minutes <= y_high):
            raise ValueError("point outside declared domain")
        column = min(columns - 1, floor((amount - x_low) * columns / (x_high - x_low)))
        row = min(rows - 1, floor((handling_minutes - y_low) * rows / (y_high - y_low)))
        counts[(column, row)] = counts.get((column, row), 0) + 1
    return counts

cells = density_cells([(47, 18), (47, 18), (81, 39)],
                      (0, 100), (0, 50), 5, 5)
assert sum(cells.values()) == 3 and max(cells.values()) == 2

Performance and operating cost

For N points and C occupied cells, fixed-grid counting takes O(N) time and O(C) memory, with C no larger than the number of grid positions. Rendering one rectangle per occupied cell can be much cheaper than rendering N circles. The example rejects out-of-domain points; a production view may instead maintain an explicit overflow bucket, but it must label that choice. Recompute bins when the axis domain or pixel resolution changes, and do not confuse screen-density counts with a probability density estimate.

Common Mistakes

  • Lowering opacity and assuming the visible marks still represent all records.
  • Sampling rare cases away while evaluating an exception-handling workflow.
  • Comparing density grids built with different bounds or cell widths.
  • Calling a fitted slope causal based on a crowded scatterplot.

Validation drill

Generate 4,700 routine handling cases plus 31 rare high-delay cases. Compare raw points, a fixed grid and a seeded stratified sample; report whether each view keeps the rare cluster visible and whether displayed counts reconcile.

title: Heatmaps: make missing cells, rates and color domains explicit
summary: Construct a complete matrix and keep unmeasured cells separate from zero-valued measurements.
body:
Construct a complete matrix and keep unmeasured cells separate from zero-valued measurements.

A cell needs two keys and one measure

A heatmap is a matrix of marks whose position comes from two discrete dimensions and whose fill encodes a value. The first decision is the unit of a cell: one depot-day, one product-hour, or one model-class pair. Build the complete expected key grid before coloring it. Otherwise an absent record disappears, compresses the layout, or is mistaken for a low value. A white cell may mean zero, unobserved, unavailable or suppressed; these states require separate labels or patterns. Calendar completeness matters when columns are days.

Rates need their denominators

A defect-rate cell with 4 defects in 8 inspections and another with 40 in 800 inspections should not be interpreted as equally reliable even if their colors reflect 50% and 5%. Carry inspected count into a tooltip, visible annotation, or companion display. If no inspections occurred, the rate is undefined rather than zero. Measure grain determines whether the numerator and denominator belong to the same cell. If filters remove rows, recompute both counts instead of averaging precomputed cell percentages.

Fix the color domain for comparison

An automatically rescaled palette can make the same value change color when the viewer filters a subset. For cross-filter or before-after comparisons, set a stable domain and show its endpoints. A sequential palette fits a nonnegative rate; a diverging palette needs a meaningful center such as zero difference or target variance. Quantile coloring gives bins with similar record counts, not equal numeric widths. Label the bin rule. Accessible encodings add text or pattern cues so the chart still works without color.

Choose ordering deliberately

Alphabetical row order is reproducible, but ordering by a stable baseline can expose patterns. Clustering rows by similarity can reveal structure yet change the question: adjacent rows no longer imply geographic or operational proximity. If an algorithm orders rows, record its input period and freeze the order for comparisons. Keep hidden categories and totals visible. A truncated matrix that shows only the busiest depots is a selected population, not the entire network. Facet-order discipline applies here too.

Test the matrix contract

Include an observed zero, a missing key, a present key with zero exposure, an invalid negative count and a high-rate low-volume cell. Confirm each has a distinct state. Check the matrix against a long-form data table with the same row and column order. On mobile, provide axis labels that remain visible while scrolling; a distant legend is not enough. Exported CSV should retain status, numerator and denominator rather than only a color code.

Worked contract

def inspection_matrix(
    observations: dict[tuple[str, str], tuple[int, int]],
    depots: list[str], days: list[str]
) -> dict[tuple[str, str], tuple[str, float | None, int | None]]:
    expected = {(depot, day) for depot in depots for day in days}
    if len(expected) != len(depots) * len(days) or set(observations) - expected:
        raise ValueError("duplicate labels or unexpected cell")
    grid = {}
    for key in expected:
        if key not in observations:
            grid[key] = ("missing", None, None)
            continue
        defects, inspected = observations[key]
        if not 0 <= defects <= inspected:
            raise ValueError("invalid cell counts")
        grid[key] = ("no-exposure", None, 0) if inspected == 0 else (
            "observed", defects / inspected, inspected)
    return grid

matrix = inspection_matrix(
    {("north", "Mon"): (0, 47), ("north", "Tue"): (0, 0)},
    ["north"], ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"])
assert matrix[("north", "Mon")] == ("observed", 0.0, 47)
assert matrix[("north", "Tue")][0] == "no-exposure"
assert matrix[("north", "Wed")][0] == "missing"

Performance and operating cost

For R row labels, C column labels and M supplied observations, building the expected grid takes O(RC + M) time and O(RC) space. Large sparse matrices should keep sparse storage and generate only visible tiles, but must still represent missing cells and axis positions correctly. The demonstration returns status, rate and denominator; a production export should also retain the numerator and source snapshot. Color scaling and rendering add work proportional to visible cells, not merely to supplied observations.

Common Mistakes

  • Assigning the same white fill to an observed zero and an absent cell.
  • Changing the color domain after filtering without warning the reader.
  • Averaging cell percentages instead of recomputing counts for a new group.
  • Sorting rows by one selected day, then describing the layout as a stable geographic order.

Validation drill

Build a depot-by-day inspection matrix with 6 depots and 17 days. Insert one missing cell, one zero-exposure cell and one observed zero. Verify their states in both chart legend and exported data.
