title: Choropleth maps: normalize counts and audit boundary coverage
summary: Join measures to the right polygons, use a stated denominator, and distinguish unmapped places from zero-valued regions.
body:
Join measures to the right polygons, use a stated denominator, and distinguish unmapped places from zero-valued regions.

Area color is not an event count

A choropleth fills geographic regions according to a measure. Large polygons occupy more pixels and can dominate attention even when they contain few people or events. Raw incident counts often track exposure, such as population or active deliveries, more than risk. For a comparable rate, carry numerator and denominator for each polygon and specify the period. Exposure-based rates explain why 8 incidents across 47,000 trips differ from 8 across 470 trips. A map can still show counts when workload is the question; label it as a count map.

Join by stable region identity

Names drift, abbreviations collide, and administrative boundaries change. Join facts to geometry with stable region IDs and a boundary version. Report unmatched fact IDs, polygons with no measure, duplicate assignments and overlapping boundaries before rendering. Spatial joins are a separate operation from coloring polygons; they can duplicate a record if geometries overlap. If one region splits midyear, a before-after map needs a common boundary basis or an explicit break. Do not let a chart library silently drop unmatched regions.

Projection and extent shape perception

A projection transforms coordinates into map space. It can distort area, shape or distance; no flat map preserves everything. For regional comparison, keep the same projection, extent and viewport across panels, and avoid interpreting the visible area of a polygon as its population. Insets for distant regions need clear labels and scale context. If exact comparison of rates matters more than location, provide a sorted bar chart alongside the map. Choose the visual that serves the question, not merely the available geometry.

Class breaks are an editorial decision

Equal-width bins, quantile bins and fixed policy thresholds answer different questions. A quantile palette can assign different colors to tiny numeric differences when many regions cluster tightly; fixed thresholds can leave some colors unused. Print numeric breakpoints and keep them stable when comparing dates. Use a separate treatment for missing data and low-exposure suppression. Color-domain rules carry over to map legends. Keep the original rate in the accessible table and tooltip; color bins are a summary, not the data.

Protect sensitive locations

Very small denominators can make rates unstable and expose information about a few people or facilities. Define a minimum publishable group size, aggregate or suppress as appropriate, and show a visible suppressed state. Do not infer that a blank region has zero risk. Location privacy and small-sample display belong to the same release review. Test a region with no geometry, a polygon with no observation, a zero numerator and a zero denominator separately.

Worked contract

def regional_rates(
    boundary_ids: set[str],
    incident_counts: dict[str, tuple[int, int]]
) -> dict[str, tuple[str, float | None]]:
    unknown = set(incident_counts) - boundary_ids
    if unknown:
        raise ValueError(f"facts without geometry: {sorted(unknown)}")
    result = {}
    for region_id in boundary_ids:
        if region_id not in incident_counts:
            result[region_id] = ("missing", None)
            continue
        incidents, trips = incident_counts[region_id]
        if not 0 <= incidents <= trips:
            raise ValueError("invalid regional counts")
        result[region_id] = ("no-exposure", None) if trips == 0 else (
            "observed", incidents / trips)
    return result

rates = regional_rates({"zone-47", "zone-81", "zone-94"},
                       {"zone-47": (8, 470), "zone-81": (0, 81)})
assert rates["zone-47"][1] == 8 / 470
assert rates["zone-81"] == ("observed", 0.0)
assert rates["zone-94"] == ("missing", None)

Performance and operating cost

For B boundary IDs and M measured regions, this join-and-rate check takes O(B + M) expected time and O(B) output space using hash sets. Rendering cost depends on polygon vertex count, projection and viewport clipping, none of which this code performs. Simplify geometry only to a documented tolerance and keep an exact source for hit tests. A cached tile or geometry file must carry the same boundary version as the measures. The code distinguishes zero and missing; a real publication layer also enforces suppression and uncertainty policy.

Common Mistakes

  • Coloring raw counts as if the map showed per-person or per-trip risk.
  • Joining on human-readable region names without checking unmatched and duplicated keys.
  • Treating a missing polygon or missing measure as zero.
  • Changing map bounds or class breaks between comparison dates.

Validation drill

Map 23 service zones with one split boundary, one missing measure and one zone below the publishable exposure threshold. Reconcile region IDs and rates before drawing polygons; add a sorted rate table for exact comparison.

title: Large chart series: reduce marks without erasing spikes
summary: Choose a visible-resolution data product and preserve first, last, minimum and maximum values in each bucket.
body:
Choose a visible-resolution data product and preserve first, last, minimum and maximum values in each bucket.

More samples than pixels need a display rule

A line chart with hundreds of thousands of readings across a 900-pixel plot cannot show each reading distinctly. Sending every point still costs transfer, parsing, memory, layout and interaction time. A random sample or every-50th-point stride can erase a brief but operationally important spike. Decide whether the reader is inspecting shape, extrema, exact intervals or anomalies. The chart task determines the reduction method. The full-resolution data remains the source; the plotted series is a deliberately derived view.

Preserve a bounded envelope

For each time bucket, retain its first, last, minimum and maximum observations, ordered by timestamp and deduplicated by identity. This keeps endpoints connected and exposes local peaks and troughs that a mean would smooth away. It is not lossless: the order of several internal turns and narrow oscillations may still be compressed. Show the bucket width or resolution when it affects interpretation, and fetch raw samples on zoom or request. If missing intervals exist, split segments before reducing; joining across a gap creates a fictional line. Gap policy applies before level of detail.

Build levels against stable data versions

Precomputed hourly, daily or pixel-width buckets must use a fixed time origin and a named aggregation function. If a late event revises an old bucket, invalidate that level together with raw data. Cache keys need range, resolution, filters, unit and source generation. A multi-resolution chart can request a coarser level during pan, then replace it with fine points after the interaction settles; label provisional rendering when it might change a decision. Serving freshness constrains what a pre-aggregated chart can claim.

Keep exactness available

Tooltips on reduced marks should describe the bucket, extrema and sample count. Calling a retained minimum a point-in-time average is wrong. A downloadable CSV should offer the filtered raw interval or clearly name the reduced level. If a user clicks a peak to investigate a machine stoppage, resolve it to source IDs rather than an arbitrary nearby display point. The export manifest should state whether the series is raw or reduced.

Measure end-to-end cost

Track transfer bytes, parse time, memory, first paint, pan latency and number of marks actually drawn. A server-side envelope can reduce browser work but adds query and cache-maintenance cost. A canvas renderer can draw many marks faster than DOM-based SVG, yet it needs deliberate keyboard and text alternatives. Test a single-sample range, identical timestamps, gaps and a narrow spike at each bucket boundary. The acceptance check is not only a speedup: the operational alert must remain visible at the default zoom.

Worked contract

def extrema_envelope(samples: list[tuple[int, float]],
                     bucket_size: int) -> list[tuple[int, float]]:
    if bucket_size < 1 or any(samples[index][0] >= samples[index + 1][0]
                               for index in range(len(samples) - 1)):
        raise ValueError("bucket size or time order is invalid")
    reduced = []
    for start in range(0, len(samples), bucket_size):
        bucket = samples[start:start + bucket_size]
        selected = {bucket[0], bucket[-1],
                    min(bucket, key=lambda point: point[1]),
                    max(bucket, key=lambda point: point[1])}
        reduced.extend(sorted(selected, key=lambda point: point[0]))
    return reduced

readings = [(47, 4.0), (48, 4.1), (49, 81.0), (50, 4.2),
            (51, 4.0), (52, 3.9)]
visible = extrema_envelope(readings, 4)
assert (49, 81.0) in visible and visible[0] == readings[0]
assert len(visible) <= 4 * ((len(readings) + 3) // 4)

Performance and operating cost

For N sorted samples and bucket size B, the demonstration runs in O(N + (N/B) log 4) time and emits at most four observations per bucket, O(N/B) output space. Python slices hold up to O(B) temporary items. It assumes strictly increasing timestamps and one continuous segment; production data with same-time events needs an explicit tie policy, and gaps need separate segments. Maintaining a pyramid of levels increases storage but can make viewport requests proportional to visible resolution rather than total history.

Common Mistakes

  • Taking every nth reading and deleting a short-lived alarm spike.
  • Reducing across a missing-data gap and drawing a continuous line.
  • Calling a retained minimum or maximum a bucket average.
  • Caching a reduced level without the filter and source-version keys.

Validation drill

Reduce a 47,000-point sensor series to a 900-pixel view. Insert 19 one-point spikes at varied bucket positions and verify every spike survives the chosen display reduction; compare load and pan times with the raw series.

title: Chart exports: carry the data, filters and render contract together
summary: Give exported images an auditable data table and a compact manifest of the choices that produced them.
body:
Give exported images an auditable data table and a compact manifest of the choices that produced them.

An image is not the full evidence

A PNG captures pixels; it does not preserve the records, filter predicates, missingness states or exact values behind them. SVG retains scalable geometry, but it can still omit the underlying analytical contract. For a decision-grade chart, export an image, a machine-readable table of plotted values and a manifest describing the query and rendering choices. The package should answer which source snapshot, cohort, units, time zone, grouping rule, axis domain, palette and code version produced the picture. Dashboard provenance supplies these ingredients; export binds them to an artifact.

Version the plotted data product

A chart may use raw events, daily aggregates or a reduced display level. The export must name that level. Include a dataset snapshot or immutable revision, plus the report's as-of time when corrections are possible. A hash of canonical manifest bytes detects accidental changes to the manifest; it does not authenticate a source by itself. If integrity across systems matters, sign the package through a trusted release path. Never include private identifiers or unmasked rows merely because a chart view was authorized. Data classification still governs exports.

Keep visible and downloadable values aligned

The CSV or JSON table must use the same filters, denominator, sort, unit and missing-value policy as the displayed chart. If the chart shows rounded percentages, include underlying counts and unrounded rates in the data export while documenting the display rounding. A tooltip, table and image title should agree on the period and finalization status. Linked filters can change the cohort moments before a user clicks export; capture one state and one data version atomically for the whole package.

Make the visual portable and accessible

An SVG is useful for vector editing and high-resolution print, but font substitution and external styles can change its appearance. A PNG is more predictable but loses scale and selectable text. Include an accessible text summary and data table in either case. Document the output size, color profile where relevant, and the scale tick labels. Text alternatives should describe the main pattern, notable exceptions and uncertainty rather than repeat a generic chart title. For a public download, test that no hidden private series remain in SVG markup or embedded metadata.

Recreate before release

Re-run the export from its manifest in a clean environment. Compare plotted counts, axis limits, filters, title, source generation and checksum, allowing only declared rendering differences such as font rasterization. A changed query definition should make an old package non-reproducible by design; report that conflict instead of silently rendering with today's code. Keep an editorial preview for review, then publish an immutable artifact reference when the chart is used in a report or audit. Reduced series need the level and bucket rule in the manifest.

Worked contract

import hashlib
import json

def chart_manifest(query_id: str, dataset_version: str,
                   filters: dict[str, list[str]],
                   axis_domain: tuple[float, float],
                   plotted_rows: int) -> tuple[dict, str]:
    if not query_id or not dataset_version or plotted_rows < 0:
        raise ValueError("missing chart identity")
    if axis_domain[0] >= axis_domain[1]:
        raise ValueError("invalid axis domain")
    manifest = {
        "query_id": query_id,
        "dataset_version": dataset_version,
        "filters": {key: sorted(set(values))
                    for key, values in sorted(filters.items())},
        "y_axis_domain": list(axis_domain),
        "plotted_rows": plotted_rows,
        "unit": "minutes",
        "render_contract": "depot-delay-v3",
    }
    payload = json.dumps(manifest, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"),
                         ensure_ascii=False).encode("utf-8")
    return manifest, hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest()

first = chart_manifest("depot-delay-week", "snapshot-81",
                       {"region": ["north", "north"]}, (0, 47), 31)
second = chart_manifest("depot-delay-week", "snapshot-81",
                        {"region": ["north"]}, (0, 47), 31)
assert first == second and len(first[1]) == 64

Performance and operating cost

For F total filter values and M serialized manifest bytes, sorting normalized filters costs O(F log F) in the worst case; JSON encoding and SHA-256 hashing take O(M) time and O(M) temporary memory. Exporting an image or plotted data can cost much more and depends on the renderer and row count. This hash identifies equal manifest bytes, not equal pixels or trustworthy provenance. Add a data-file checksum and a signed release record when the export package crosses a trust boundary.

Common Mistakes

  • Publishing only a screenshot when reviewers need the plotted data and cohort definition.
  • Exporting a CSV from a stale filter state while the chart shows a newer selection.
  • Assuming a manifest hash proves who created the data.
  • Embedding hidden private rows in an otherwise public SVG or HTML export.

Validation drill

Export one filtered depot-delay chart as SVG and CSV with a manifest. Change only the filter and verify the manifest digest changes, then rebuild the original chart from its saved version and compare counts and axis bounds.

title: Paired-change charts: match entities before drawing a slope
summary: Use slope and dumbbell views only after the before-and-after population is reconciled.
body:
Use slope and dumbbell views only after the before-and-after population is reconciled.

The line encodes identity

A slope chart connects two measurements for the same entity. Its line claims a valid pair, not just two values with matching labels. If a store was renamed, split or absent in one period, resolve that identity before drawing. A join on display name can connect unrelated stores, while a broad outer join can make missing endpoints look like zero. Join cardinality should be checked at one row per entity and period. Record which entities were excluded from the paired population.

Choose difference or ratio deliberately

A dumbbell chart places two points on a shared quantitative scale; a slope chart emphasizes direction between endpoints. The axis unit and baseline decide whether a move appears large. A change from 47 to 81 is 34 units and about 72 percent of the starting value, but those answer different questions. For baseline zero, a percentage change is undefined. State which measure is encoded by the sorted order and put exact start, end and difference in accessible text. Axis rules apply to both forms.

Control clutter and crossings

With dozens of entities, labels and crossing segments become hard to follow. Sort by one declared endpoint or difference, keep label positions consistent, and consider small multiples or a ranked difference bar when comparison is more important than identity tracking. Highlight selected entities without fading the rest into illegibility. A connected pair should use a line style, endpoint labels or shape in addition to color. Accessible encodings matter when the positive and negative groups share a palette.

Check comparability across periods

Before-after values may use different denominator definitions, currencies, coverage windows or measurement instruments. Do not join a complete prior quarter to an incomplete current quarter. Record the cohort cutoff and period length. If the chart includes only entities observed in both periods, say how many were lost and whether they differ from those retained; survivorship can reverse the narrative. Provisional-period handling also applies when there are only two points.

Worked contract

def paired_depot_change(
    prior: dict[str, int | None], current: dict[str, int | None]
) -> tuple[list[tuple[str, int, int, int]], set[str]]:
    if any(value is not None and value < 0 for value in [*prior.values(), *current.values()]):
        raise ValueError("negative request count")
    matched = []
    excluded = set(prior) | set(current)
    for depot_id in sorted(set(prior) & set(current)):
        before, after = prior[depot_id], current[depot_id]
        if before is None or after is None:
            continue
        matched.append((depot_id, before, after, after - before))
        excluded.remove(depot_id)
    return matched, excluded

pairs, absent = paired_depot_change(
    {"depot-47": 47, "depot-81": 81, "depot-94": 31},
    {"depot-47": 81, "depot-81": None, "depot-109": 40})
assert pairs == [("depot-47", 47, 81, 34)]
assert absent == {"depot-81", "depot-94", "depot-109"}

Performance and operating cost

For P prior and C current entities, hash-set intersection and validation take O(P + C) expected time; sorting K matched IDs takes O(K log K), with O(P + C) temporary space. If an ordered warehouse query already supplies stable IDs, sorting can be handled upstream. The excluded set is part of the chart contract; deleting it to make the visualization tidy hides selection bias. A renderer still needs label-collision handling for crowded panels.

Common Mistakes

  • Connecting two stores with the same display name but different stable IDs.
  • Substituting zero for a missing endpoint.
  • Showing a percentage increase when the baseline is zero.
  • Ignoring entities absent from the second period when describing the population.

Validation drill

Compare 47 depots across two quarters. Plant a renamed depot, a split depot and four incomplete current-quarter records; reconcile identity and report matched and excluded counts before drawing slopes.

title: Empirical CDFs: read thresholds and tails without choosing bins
summary: Construct a cumulative distribution from observed values, preserving ties and sample size.
body:
Construct a cumulative distribution from observed values, preserving ties and sample size.

The step answers a threshold question

An empirical cumulative distribution function, or ECDF, gives the fraction of observed values less than or equal to each threshold. A point at 47 minutes and 0.8 means 80 percent of observations took at most 47 minutes. Unlike a histogram, it needs no bin width, so comparisons across groups are less sensitive to display choices. It still depends on the population, missing-value policy and observation window. Distribution plots should expose those rules before any percentile is interpreted.

Ties produce one jump

Repeated measurements at the same value create one larger step. If 31 of 81 jobs finish at exactly 12 minutes, the ECDF rises by 31/81 there; do not create a fake continuous slope between identical values. To compute a nearest-rank percentile, choose the first observed value whose cumulative share meets or exceeds the requested probability. Other quantile conventions interpolate and can return a number no job achieved. State the convention, especially for service targets. Sampling rules determine whether a percentile describes all jobs or a selected frame.

Keep the tail visible

Most observations can cluster near a short duration while a few long delays drive customer pain. An ECDF makes the proportion under a service threshold easy to read, but the far-right tail may still be squeezed by the axis. Add an inset, tail table or direct threshold counts when the rare cases matter. A survival-style complementary curve, one minus the ECDF, answers what fraction exceeds a threshold; be clear about strict versus inclusive inequalities at ties. Small samples need counts beside smooth-looking curves.

Compare only compatible cohorts

Two curves can differ because of case mix, eligibility, time window or measurement precision. Use consistent axis limits and units, label sample sizes, and show whether pending cases were excluded or censored. A naive ECDF of only completed jobs makes the slow unfinished work disappear. For a queue with unresolved jobs, use an analysis that handles censoring or restrict the claim to completed jobs. Observation status is part of the underlying data, not a cosmetic legend choice.

Worked contract

from math import ceil, isfinite

def completion_ecdf(minutes: list[float]) -> list[tuple[float, int, float]]:
    if not minutes or any(not isfinite(value) or value < 0 for value in minutes):
        raise ValueError("need finite nonnegative durations")
    ordered = sorted(minutes)
    steps = []
    for value in ordered:
        if steps and steps[-1][0] == value:
            steps[-1] = (value, steps[-1][1] + 1, 0.0)
        else:
            steps.append((value, 1, 0.0))
    cumulative = 0
    result = []
    for value, tied, _ in steps:
        cumulative += tied
        result.append((value, tied, cumulative / len(ordered)))
    return result

durations = [12, 12, 31, 47, 81]
curve = completion_ecdf(durations)
nearest_rank_80 = sorted(durations)[ceil(0.8 * len(durations)) - 1]
assert curve[0] == (12, 2, 0.4)
assert curve[-1][2] == 1.0 and nearest_rank_80 == 47

Performance and operating cost

Sorting N durations costs O(N log N) time and O(N) space for the ordered copy and output; scanning ties is O(N). Already-sorted warehouse output avoids the local sort. A chart with many distinct observations may still need visual reduction at screen resolution, but threshold queries should use the exact ordered values. The simple ECDF treats every supplied duration as complete and equally weighted; it is not a censored-data estimator.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading a completed-only ECDF as the distribution of all started jobs.
  • Treating a large jump at a tied value as a renderer defect.
  • Quoting a percentile without its sample size and quantile convention.
  • Moving axis bounds between cohorts and comparing apparent steepness.

Validation drill

Build curves for two depot cohorts of 47 and 81 completed cases. Include repeated durations and unresolved work, then report the fraction within 31 minutes and exactly which cases were excluded.

title: Sankey diagrams: reconcile flows before sizing links
summary: Make every stage transition accountable, including dropouts and unobserved destinations.
body:
Make every stage transition accountable, including dropouts and unobserved destinations.

A link represents a transfer

A Sankey diagram uses link width to encode quantity moving between stages. The visual claim is stronger than a list of counts: a unit leaving one stage must either enter a named next stage, exit the process, or remain unobserved under a declared cutoff. If 81 claims enter triage and 47 reach review, the other 34 need a visible destination, not an unexplained gap. Unit-of-analysis rules prevent one claim with multiple events from becoming several flows.

Give nodes stage-specific identities

The same label at two stages does not necessarily describe the same state. Use stable stage and state IDs, deduplicate by entity and transition, and decide how repeated or backward transitions are handled. A diagram that assumes a directed acyclic process can fail when work returns to triage. In that case, either aggregate one chosen journey window or use another graph view that represents loops. Network diagrams can show cycles, though they answer a different question.

Check conservation at intermediate stages

For a closed interval, incoming and outgoing measured quantities at a transit state should balance after explicit additions, losses and stock change. If 47 enter review and 42 leave, five may still be in progress; add a pending exit or annotate the stock. For a live interval, arrivals and departures can differ because the cohort has not matured. Attach extraction time and observation horizon to the flow, and never compare incoming of one cohort to outgoing of another. Provisional periods need separate handling.

Make ordering and scale inspectable

Link crossing is partly a layout choice. Reordering nodes can reduce crossings without changing the data, so visual proximity must not be treated as a causal relation. Show quantities, units and denominators in text or a companion table. Fixed link colors can track origin across stages, but blending may obscure a small branch; direct labels or hover summaries help. Accessible alternatives should list source, target and value. Large graphs may be better as a transition table.

Worked contract

from collections import defaultdict

def reconcile_flow(
    links: list[tuple[str, str, int]], transit_nodes: set[str]
) -> dict[str, tuple[int, int]]:
    incoming = defaultdict(int)
    outgoing = defaultdict(int)
    for source, target, quantity in links:
        if not source or not target or quantity < 0:
            raise ValueError("invalid flow link")
        outgoing[source] += quantity
        incoming[target] += quantity
    balances = {node: (incoming[node], outgoing[node]) for node in transit_nodes}
    if any(entered != left for entered, left in balances.values()):
        raise ValueError(f"unreconciled transit node: {balances}")
    return balances

journey = [("intake", "review", 47),
           ("intake", "unobserved-exit", 34),
           ("review", "closed", 42),
           ("review", "pending", 5)]
assert reconcile_flow(journey, {"review"}) == {"review": (47, 47)}
assert sum(value for source, _, value in journey if source == "intake") == 81

Performance and operating cost

For E links and T transit nodes, accumulation and reconciliation take O(E + T) expected time and O(V) space for V encountered nodes. Layout can be substantially more expensive and depends on the rendering algorithm; do not mix that cost with the inexpensive accounting check. A real workflow also checks duplicate entity transitions and whether stock change belongs in the diagram. The example treats all links as counts in one cohort and one period.

Common Mistakes

  • Hiding exits to make the main path look complete.
  • Counting multiple events from one entity as separate stage transfers.
  • Balancing one period's arrivals against another period's departures.
  • Assuming node position or link crossing has business meaning.

Validation drill

Model 81 claims through intake, review and closure. Add a pending branch and an unobserved exit; fail the reconciliation when either is removed, then render a transition table beside the flow.

title: Network graphs: define nodes and edges before trusting the layout
summary: Check identity, direction, duplicates and degree before placing nodes on a canvas.
body:
Check identity, direction, duplicates and degree before placing nodes on a canvas.

The edge is the claim

A node-link graph represents entities and relationships. Before running a force layout, specify whether an edge means a message, a transaction, a dependency or a co-occurrence, and whether direction matters. Two messages from depot A to depot B may be two events or one weighted relationship. Resolve that choice at the declared grain. Stable node IDs prevent two accounts with the same display name from merging. The unit of analysis extends to graph edges.

Layout distance is not a metric

Force layouts position nodes by an algorithm balancing constraints. Nearby nodes may be strongly connected, but the distance is not automatically a business quantity; changing a random seed, viewport or graph subset can move them. Pin important positions or show a fixed comparison layout when inspecting versions. Report quantitative graph measures separately with their definitions. Comparison panels should preserve a stable node identity and comparable viewport.

Count what selection removes

A filtered network can make a high-degree node appear isolated if many of its neighbors are hidden. Show selected and total degree separately or state that the graph describes only the visible subgraph. Validate dangling edges whose endpoints are absent; do not let the renderer silently discard them. For large graphs, aggregate by a declared community or show a ranked adjacency table, because a dense hairball hides paths and edge direction. Resolution limits apply to edges and nodes as much as to points in a chart.

Design for inspection

Hover-only relationships are inaccessible on touch and keyboard. Provide a searchable node list, ordered neighbor table, edge direction labels and a way to inspect an entity without relying on color. Keep private identifiers out of public graph exports. A link of width 8 should name the weight unit and time interval; do not use width for one measure and tooltip for another. Text alternatives carry exact relationships that an overview cannot show.

Worked contract

from collections import defaultdict

def directed_degrees(
    node_ids: set[str], links: list[tuple[str, str, int]]
) -> dict[str, tuple[int, int]]:
    if not node_ids:
        raise ValueError("empty node set")
    incoming = defaultdict(int)
    outgoing = defaultdict(int)
    for source, target, weight in links:
        if source not in node_ids or target not in node_ids or weight <= 0:
            raise ValueError("dangling edge or nonpositive weight")
        outgoing[source] += weight
        incoming[target] += weight
    return {node: (incoming[node], outgoing[node]) for node in node_ids}

degrees = directed_degrees(
    {"depot-47", "depot-81", "depot-94"},
    [("depot-47", "depot-81", 31),
     ("depot-81", "depot-94", 8)])
assert degrees["depot-81"] == (31, 8)
assert sum(value[0] for value in degrees.values()) == 39

Performance and operating cost

For V nodes and E links, endpoint validation and weighted-degree counting take O(V + E) expected time and O(V) space. Layout may take many iterative passes and dominate CPU; this accounting step should run first so bad graph data does not get disguised by an attractive arrangement. The function sums weights and permits repeated directed pairs by design. If the chart promises one edge per pair, aggregate and count duplicates explicitly before layout.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating screen distance from a force layout as an exact relationship strength.
  • Discarding edges with missing endpoints without an audit count.
  • Mixing event count with unique-neighbor degree.
  • Comparing two filtered layouts without identifying removed nodes and edges.

Validation drill

Map handoffs among 31 service teams. Add a duplicate label, a dangling edge and a filtered-out hub; preserve stable IDs and report both visible and full-graph weighted degrees.

title: Chart annotations: align events to the right clock without claiming causality
summary: Treat deployment lines, policy changes and outages as versioned data with time windows and uncertainty.
body:
Treat deployment lines, policy changes and outages as versioned data with time windows and uncertainty.

An annotation is another dataset

A vertical line on a chart often marks a deployment, policy change or outage. That event has its own timestamp, time zone, scope, source and uncertainty. A release may roll through regions over several hours; drawing one instant across all regions invents precision. Model it as a window or per-region events, then map it to the same clock as the measured series. The time-series clock must be settled before annotations are placed.

Scope must match the measured population

If only one depot received a new workflow, an all-depot annotation can imply that every plotted change followed the intervention. Filter event records by affected site, product and population, and expose the scope in the label. Preserve events outside the visible interval in the export but do not draw them in the viewport. Distinguish a data outage from a true operational incident: both can create a cliff, but only one is a measured outcome. Population contracts determine whether a note belongs on a chart.

Timing does not prove effect

A change in the curve after a marked event may be coincidence, seasonality, a denominator shift or a delayed measurement. Write labels such as 'workflow enabled' rather than 'workflow improved response time' unless a separate analysis supports the latter. If an effect is being estimated, show the design, comparison group and uncertainty elsewhere. Effect-size analysis is distinct from descriptive annotation. Keep the event visible even when the post-event result disappoints expectations.

Avoid collision and preserve provenance

Several events on one day can produce overlapping labels. Group them in a visible list keyed to markers, prioritizing material scope and preserving access to every event. The annotation export should include event ID, earliest and latest time, scope, label and source version. A revised event time should update the chart and its manifest together. Reproducible exports need both series and annotation versions. Test daylight-saving boundaries and a deployment window that straddles the chart's range.

Worked contract

from datetime import datetime, timezone

def visible_events(
    events: list[tuple[str, datetime, datetime, set[str]]],
    view_start: datetime, view_end: datetime, depot_id: str
) -> list[str]:
    if view_start.tzinfo is None or view_end.tzinfo is None or view_start >= view_end:
        raise ValueError("invalid aware view interval")
    selected = []
    for event_id, began, ended, depots in events:
        if not event_id or began.tzinfo is None or ended.tzinfo is None or began >= ended:
            raise ValueError("invalid event interval")
        if depot_id in depots and began < view_end and ended > view_start:
            selected.append(event_id)
    return selected

utc = timezone.utc
window = [("release-47", datetime(2026, 8, 11, 9, tzinfo=utc),
           datetime(2026, 8, 11, 11, tzinfo=utc), {"north"})]
assert visible_events(window, datetime(2026, 8, 11, 10, tzinfo=utc),
                      datetime(2026, 8, 12, tzinfo=utc), "north") == ["release-47"]
assert visible_events(window, datetime(2026, 8, 11, 10, tzinfo=utc),
                      datetime(2026, 8, 12, tzinfo=utc), "south") == []

Performance and operating cost

Scanning E events is O(E) time and O(M) output space for M matching IDs. An indexed event store can narrow by time and scope for many dashboards. The example uses half-open display intervals and event windows, so a window ending exactly at the view start is excluded. It does not infer causality or validate whether a deployment reached every unit in its declared scope; those are separate evidence checks.

Common Mistakes

  • Drawing a gradual rollout as one global instant.
  • Annotating all depots with an event that affected only one.
  • Writing a causal outcome claim in an event label without a study.
  • Failing to version corrected event times alongside the plotted series.

Validation drill

Annotate a 29-day response-time chart with three region-specific rollouts, one data outage and one event that crosses the visible interval boundary. Verify the right events appear for each region and export their time windows.

title: Box and violin charts: compare groups without inventing density
summary: Keep sample size, quartiles and bandwidth visible when a smoothed shape represents observations.
body:
Keep sample size, quartiles and bandwidth visible when a smoothed shape represents observations.

Begin with observations

A box summarizes a group's quartiles and median; a violin adds an estimated density shape. Neither replaces the sample size. A smooth violin made from seven delivery times can look as confident as one made from seven thousand. Put each group's count beside its label and show individual points for small groups. Distribution and outlier displays explain what the summary hides. First check whether groups cover the same window, unit and eligibility rule. Otherwise the apparent difference may be a cohort change.

Declare the quartile rule

Software packages can interpolate quartiles differently, and whiskers may mean the extrema or a multiple of the interquartile range. State the rule in the chart caption or export record. A point beyond a whisker is not automatically bad data; it is flagged under that rule. If the decision needs the fraction exceeding a service threshold, calculate that fraction directly rather than asking a box to imply it. An empirical CDF answers threshold questions without a smoothing choice.

Treat bandwidth as a parameter

A violin's width depends on a density estimate and its bandwidth. A wide bandwidth can merge two real modes; a narrow one can turn routine noise into several peaks. Compare more than one defensible bandwidth, retain a rug or points, and do not imply that a thin tail continues beyond a physical limit. The mirrored shape is a drawing convention, not a second population. Normalize violin widths by count only if width should carry count. Otherwise make widths equal and show counts separately. Grain and denominator still matter.

Keep groups comparable

Use the same quantitative axis, bandwidth rule and density normalization across groups. Truncating each group to its own range can make spreads seem alike. For latency data, inspect zeros, censored values and caps before estimating density. If the data include repeated readings from the same device, an independent violin discards pairing. A paired view retains it. Supply a text table with each count, median, quartiles and threshold exceedance for readers who cannot use the shape.

Worked contract

def quartile_summary(readings: list[float]) -> dict[str, float | int]:
    from math import isfinite
    if not readings or any(not isfinite(value) for value in readings):
        raise ValueError("readings must be finite and nonempty")
    ordered = sorted(readings)
    def midpoint(values: list[float]) -> float:
        middle = len(values) // 2
        return (values[middle] if len(values) % 2 else
                (values[middle - 1] + values[middle]) / 2)
    middle = len(ordered) // 2
    lower = ordered[:middle]
    upper = ordered[middle + len(ordered) % 2:]
    return {"count": len(ordered), "median": midpoint(ordered),
            "q1": midpoint(lower) if lower else ordered[0],
            "q3": midpoint(upper) if upper else ordered[0]}

depot_latency = quartile_summary([47, 51, 59, 68, 81, 83, 96])
assert depot_latency == {"count": 7, "median": 68, "q1": 51, "q3": 83}

Performance and operating cost

Sorting N observations costs O(N log N) time and O(N) storage for the ordered copy. A chart with G groups repeats this per group; density estimation adds work set by the estimator and evaluation grid. The code declares a median-of-halves quartile convention and handles a one-item group. It does not draw a violin or claim that seven points support a smooth density. Store the exact convention with the exported summary.

Common Mistakes

  • Drawing a smooth violin for a tiny group without points.
  • Comparing boxes whose whiskers use different rules.
  • Treating a flagged point as an invalid measurement.
  • Changing density bandwidth between groups and reading widths as a real difference.

Validation drill

Compare response times for three depots with 7, 47 and 810 records. Print each count, median and quartile rule; draw points for the smallest group, then inspect whether two bandwidth choices alter the visual claim.

title: Correlation heatmaps: show pairwise coverage before interpreting color
summary: Keep a correlation matrix honest about missing pairs, redundant cells and feature order.
body:
Keep a correlation matrix honest about missing pairs, redundant cells and feature order.

The matrix has more than coefficients

A correlation cell describes observations shared by two variables. With missing fields, one cell may use 810 records and another 47; identical color saturation hides that difference. Carry a second matrix of pairwise counts and expose it in labels, tooltips or a companion table. A blank pair means insufficient shared records or an undefined statistic, not zero association. Missing-cell rules distinguish these states. Record which rows passed eligibility filters before calculating either matrix.

Choose a missing-data contract

Pairwise deletion uses every available pair but can give each cell a different population. Complete-case deletion holds one population constant but may discard most records and change who remains. State the choice and counts. A constant column has zero variance and no Pearson correlation; mark it undefined. Do not fill its cell with zero merely to complete a square. Dataset grain and join checks should precede calculation so duplicated rows do not inflate confidence.

Order features for the reading task

Alphabetical order is stable and auditable. A domain order groups related measures. Data-driven clustering can reveal blocks, but the clustering method and input matrix become part of the result; changing order between periods makes comparison harder. Fix order for side-by-side charts, or record the exact order for each export. Show a legend centered on zero with identical limits in every panel. Scale integrity prevents a weak coefficient from receiving the same shade as a strong one elsewhere.

Do not infer a mechanism

A large coefficient can arise from shared time trends, repeated entities, selection or a third variable. The matrix is a screen for questions, not proof that changing one field changes another. Confirm striking cells with paired scatter plots, units and source counts; outliers can dominate a linear coefficient. Avoid painting both triangles when space is tight, since the duplicate area adds no information. Dense scatter views help inspect what the matrix compressed. Describe the population and time range beside every matrix.

Worked contract

from math import sqrt

def pearson_pair(records: list[dict[str, float | None]],
                 left: str, right: str) -> tuple[float | None, int]:
    pairs = [(record[left], record[right]) for record in records
             if record.get(left) is not None and record.get(right) is not None]
    count = len(pairs)
    if count < 2:
        return None, count
    left_mean = sum(value[0] for value in pairs) / count
    right_mean = sum(value[1] for value in pairs) / count
    cross = sum((x - left_mean) * (y - right_mean) for x, y in pairs)
    left_square = sum((x - left_mean) ** 2 for x, _ in pairs)
    right_square = sum((y - right_mean) ** 2 for _, y in pairs)
    if not left_square or not right_square:
        return None, count
    return cross / sqrt(left_square * right_square), count

shipments = [{"distance": 47, "cost": 81},
             {"distance": 59, "cost": 97},
             {"distance": 71, "cost": 113},
             {"distance": 83, "cost": None}]
coefficient, paired_count = pearson_pair(shipments, "distance", "cost")
assert round(coefficient, 12) == 1 and paired_count == 3

Performance and operating cost

For P fields and N rows, a direct full matrix performs O(P²N) pair work and stores O(P²) coefficients and counts. Columnar execution can lower constant costs, but pairwise coverage still needs explicit accounting. The example returns undefined for insufficient pairs or constant values and does not provide a significance test. A precise coefficient on three shared rows is weak evidence for a broad population claim.

Common Mistakes

  • Showing a coefficient without its pairwise record count.
  • Coloring undefined correlations as zero.
  • Changing row order across comparison periods without notice.
  • Treating a strong correlation as a causal intervention result.

Validation drill

Build a five-field matrix where one field appears in only 47 of 810 records. Show the count matrix beside the coefficient matrix, then compare pairwise and complete-case populations.

title: Forecast fan charts: label interval meaning and forecast horizon
summary: Separate observed history from forecasts and keep coverage claims attached to their method.
body:
Separate observed history from forecasts and keep coverage claims attached to their method.

A band needs a named quantity

A shaded region around a forecast could show uncertainty in an estimated mean, uncertainty for a future individual outcome, or a range of scenarios. These are different claims. A future-observation prediction interval is usually wider than an interval for the mean under the same model assumptions. Label the target, coverage level and calibration period. Uncertainty displays should also expose sample size and unstable estimates. Color alone must not carry the difference between observed and projected values.

Mark the boundary

Draw the last observed time as a visible boundary and use a different line style for forecasts. A continuous line through that boundary can make modeled values look measured. Do not fill missing observed dates with predictions and call the whole line history. Time-series gap rules still govern the observed segment. State whether the first future period is a complete day, week or fiscal interval, especially when a dashboard refreshes mid-period.

Nested bands need checks

A fan chart may show 50, 80 and 95 percent intervals. At each horizon, narrower bands must sit inside wider ones. The lower bound may fall and the upper bound may rise as coverage increases. Check containment in the data before rendering. Wider horizons often have wider uncertainty, but that shape is not guaranteed for every conditioned model or bounded target. Never widen bands by hand for appearance. The export should retain interval definition, model version and generation time.

Backtest the claim

If an interval claims 80 percent coverage, compare past issued intervals with realized values at a fixed forecast horizon and documented window. Count misses alongside nominal coverage. A recent shock or measurement change can break earlier calibration. An 80 percent band is not a promise that exactly eight of every ten future points must land inside it; coverage is assessed across repeated forecasts under stated conditions. Event annotations can mark changed processes without proving their cause.

Worked contract

def validate_fan_rows(rows: list[dict]) -> None:
    previous_horizon = -1
    for row in rows:
        horizon = row["horizon"]
        if not isinstance(horizon, int) or horizon <= previous_horizon:
            raise ValueError("horizons must increase")
        previous_horizon = horizon
        center = row["forecast"]
        inner = row["interval_50"]
        outer = row["interval_80"]
        if not (outer[0] <= inner[0] <= center <= inner[1] <= outer[1]):
            raise ValueError("intervals must nest around forecast")

issued_forecast = [
    {"horizon": 1, "forecast": 81,
     "interval_50": (75, 87), "interval_80": (68, 94)},
    {"horizon": 2, "forecast": 83,
     "interval_50": (74, 92), "interval_80": (62, 104)},
]
validate_fan_rows(issued_forecast)
assert issued_forecast[1]["interval_80"][1] == 104

Performance and operating cost

Validation scans H horizons in O(H) time and O(1) additional space. Rendering nested bands scales with horizons times interval levels. The check verifies ordering and containment only; it cannot establish empirical coverage, calibration or model quality. Finite numeric values and exact time-zone handling also need validation at the source boundary before a production forecast is issued.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling a mean-confidence band a future-observation prediction interval.
  • Drawing forecast points with the same style as measurements.
  • Allowing an 80 percent band to cross inside its 50 percent band.
  • Claiming nominal coverage without checking past issued forecasts against outcomes.

Validation drill

Issue 47 weekly forecasts with saved 50 and 80 percent bounds. Mark the observed-to-forecast boundary, validate every nested interval, and report realized coverage at horizons one and four separately.

title: Hexbin density: count overlapping points without hiding exposure
summary: Declare coordinates, bin resolution and whether color means count or rate.
body:
Declare coordinates, bin resolution and whether color means count or rate.

Overplotting is a counting problem

When thousands of marks overlap, a dark patch can reflect drawing order or opacity rather than a trustworthy count. Binning makes the count explicit. A hexagonal grid offers a compact neighborhood shape, but it still imposes a resolution and origin. Record both. Overplotting and sampling bias explain why a random sample may help inspection but cannot silently replace total-density reporting. Show how many points survived filtering and coordinate validation before any bins are painted.

Coordinate units determine the grid

A grid in longitude and latitude degrees does not represent equal ground area across latitudes. For a geographic density question, project coordinates into an appropriate metric system before choosing cell width. If this is only a relative screen-space view, say so and avoid claims about area-normalized risk. Keep projection, extent and grid origin fixed across time panels. Otherwise unchanged points may fall into different cells. Geographic rate maps have a related denominator problem.

Count and exposure answer different questions

A cell with 81 incidents may cover 810,000 journeys; a cell with 47 may cover 4,700. Count highlights workload, while incidents per journey describe a different quantity. Preserve zero-exposure cells separately from zero-incident cells. Dividing by drawn polygon area does not produce a population risk. The denominator contract must match the decision. If sparse cells are suppressed for privacy, label that suppression and retain a public aggregate total rather than pretending the hidden cells are zero.

Test resolution and edge effects

A coarse grid can merge two nearby clusters; a fine grid can fragment one. Inspect multiple declared widths while keeping the color domain comparable. Points exactly on the extent edge need a documented inclusion rule. Export each bin's identifier, center or polygon, count, exposure and suppression state so the chart can be checked without its pixels. The export manifest should retain projection, extent, width and origin. An accessible summary should identify the highest-count cells and explain the unit encoded by color.

Worked contract

from collections import Counter
from math import floor, isfinite

def audit_spatial_counts(points: list[tuple[float, float]],
                         cell_width: float) -> Counter[tuple[int, int]]:
    if not isfinite(cell_width) or cell_width <= 0:
        raise ValueError("cell width must be positive")
    if any(not isfinite(x) or not isfinite(y) for x, y in points):
        raise ValueError("coordinates must be finite")
    return Counter((floor(x / cell_width), floor(y / cell_width))
                   for x, y in points)

depot_coordinates = [(47.2, 81.6), (47.7, 81.1), (59.4, 81.5)]
audit = audit_spatial_counts(depot_coordinates, 4)
assert audit[(11, 20)] == 2 and sum(audit.values()) == 3

Performance and operating cost

This rectangular audit grid takes O(N) expected time and O(B) space for N points and B occupied bins. It checks count conservation before passing projected coordinates to a hexbin renderer; rectangular cells and hexagons do not share identifiers. The renderer decides hexagon placement and edge rules. A real map also needs projection and exposure joins versioned with its bin table. Preserve input and retained counts to detect losses.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling raw incident counts a risk rate.
  • Using degree-based cells as if they had equal ground area.
  • Changing grid extent between periods and interpreting bin movement as behavior change.
  • Hiding suppressed or zero-exposure cells as ordinary zero counts.

Validation drill

Bin 810 projected service calls at two widths. Reconcile counts to input, attach journey exposure by cell and compare the busiest cell with the highest incident-rate cell.

title: Diverging bars: put signed differences on one shared zero
summary: Choose a meaningful reference, keep a shared scale and retain both values behind every gap.
body:
Choose a meaningful reference, keep a shared scale and retain both values behind every gap.

The reference is the argument

A diverging bar begins at zero and extends according to a signed difference. That zero must mean something: actual minus plan, current minus prior, or group A minus group B. Put the formula and unit near the axis. A negative result may mean a shortfall, a benefit or simply a lower measurement. Label the groups rather than assuming red always means bad. A shared baseline lets readers compare directions.

Keep both operands available

A difference of 34 could arise from 47 versus 81 or 4,700 versus 4,734. The same bar length does not reveal operational scale. Tooltips and exports should contain both values, the reference version and any denominator used to make a rate. If teams differ sharply in size, a rate difference may answer the comparison better than counts. Denominator design precedes color choice. A gap based on a missing or zero denominator is undefined, not a zero-length bar.

Sort for the decision

Ranking by signed difference groups shortfalls; ranking by absolute difference surfaces the largest departures in either direction. State the sort key. Do not reorder every small multiple independently if the reader must follow the same entity through time. Shared facet order preserves identity. For equal comparison of positive and negative magnitudes, set a symmetric numeric domain around zero. An asymmetric domain can compress one side. Never clip a long bar without an exact value label and visible break.

Expose uncertainty

A small bar near zero may be noise rather than stable movement. For estimates, add an interval marker and explain whether it crosses zero. The chart should not declare every positive value a success. A materiality threshold belongs on the plot only when its rule is documented and consistent across entities. Small-sample uncertainty matters most near the boundary. Include a text alternative listing signed gaps, both operands and the largest departures on either side.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def signed_plan_gaps(rows: list[tuple[str, float, float]]
                     ) -> list[tuple[str, float, float, float]]:
    names = [name for name, _, _ in rows]
    if len(names) != len(set(names)) or any(not name for name in names):
        raise ValueError("entity names must be unique and nonempty")
    if any(not isfinite(actual) or not isfinite(plan)
           for _, actual, plan in rows):
        raise ValueError("measurements must be finite")
    return sorted(((name, actual, plan, actual - plan)
                   for name, actual, plan in rows), key=lambda item: item[3])

depot_gaps = signed_plan_gaps([("north", 47, 81),
                              ("south", 113, 97),
                              ("west", 59, 59)])
assert depot_gaps[0] == ("north", 47, 81, -34)
assert depot_gaps[-1][3] == 16

Performance and operating cost

For N entities, computing differences takes O(N) time and sorting takes O(N log N) time with O(N) output space. Reusing order across facets avoids repeated sort decisions, though it may make one panel less locally ranked. The example calculates absolute signed differences. A rate gap needs validated denominators and a declared unit before plotting. A chart library's autoscale should not override a specified symmetric domain.

Common Mistakes

  • Coloring negative bars as bad when lower is preferable.
  • Discarding the actual and plan values after calculating a gap.
  • Using unequal left and right scales to exaggerate one direction.
  • Confusing percentage-point change with percent change.

Validation drill

Plot 47 depots' actual-minus-plan gaps. Sort by signed difference, show both operands, then compare that ranking to a rate-gap view based on eligible volume.

title: P charts: account for varying denominators before flagging a rate
summary: Use a declared baseline and period-specific limits for binomial proportions, then investigate signals without inventing causes.
body:
Use a declared baseline and period-specific limits for binomial proportions, then investigate signals without inventing causes.

A rate needs its opportunity count

A p chart follows a proportion such as defective shipments divided by inspected shipments. Forty-seven defects in 470 inspections and 47 in 4,700 do not carry the same sampling uncertainty. Plot the period denominator or put it in a table, and calculate limits from the baseline proportion using each period's sample size. Denominator discipline is the first check. Do not mix units such as orders and line items, or change the defect definition midway through the series.

Freeze the baseline before judging a new point

Choose a stable historical interval and document excluded outages, policy changes and incomplete periods. Pool baseline defects over baseline opportunities for a center line. Calculating a fresh center from every newly flagged point can move the goalposts. A period beyond an approximate three-standard-error limit is a signal to investigate; it does not prove a specific cause. Event annotations should distinguish observed timing from causal evidence. A confirmed process change may justify a new baseline, but record where the old phase ends.

Know the approximation's limits

The simple p-chart formula assumes independent, comparable Bernoulli opportunities and a fairly stable underlying probability. Correlated batches, rare events or extra variation can make the limits misleading. Tiny sample sizes produce wide limits; values must still stay between zero and one. If repeated points reveal more variation than the model allows, investigate the collection process or choose a method suited to overdispersion. Small-sample displays help communicate why a large-looking percentage swing may be weak evidence. A control limit is not a target or a confidence interval for a business decision.

Explain the chart without color

Show the center line, period-specific bounds, actual rate, numerator and denominator in the export. Mark flagged points with shape and text, not red alone. If a late-arriving batch changes a historical numerator, recompute the affected point and disclose the revision. Provisional periods should be clearly separate from finalized ones. An accessible summary can state which periods crossed limits and which lacked enough data, while leaving the causal diagnosis to the investigation.

Worked contract

from math import sqrt

def p_chart_rows(baseline: list[tuple[int, int]],
                 periods: list[tuple[str, int, int]]
                 ) -> list[tuple[str, float, float, float, bool]]:
    def valid(defects: int, inspected: int) -> bool:
        return (isinstance(defects, int) and isinstance(inspected, int)
                and inspected > 0 and 0 <= defects <= inspected)
    if not baseline or any(not valid(d, n) for d, n in baseline):
        raise ValueError("baseline requires valid defect counts")
    if any(not label or not valid(d, n) for label, d, n in periods):
        raise ValueError("period counts or labels are invalid")
    center = sum(d for d, _ in baseline) / sum(n for _, n in baseline)
    output = []
    for label, defects, inspected in periods:
        radius = 3 * sqrt(center * (1 - center) / inspected)
        lower, upper = max(0.0, center - radius), min(1.0, center + radius)
        rate = defects / inspected
        output.append((label, rate, lower, upper, rate < lower or rate > upper))
    return output

baseline = [(47, 470), (59, 590), (81, 810)]
signals = p_chart_rows(baseline, [("week-47", 47, 470),
                                  ("week-48", 3, 470)])
assert round(signals[0][1], 4) == 0.1
assert signals[1][-1] is True

Performance and operating cost

For B baseline periods and P plotted periods, this calculation takes O(B+P) time and O(P) output space. The three-standard-error limits are an approximation under an independent binomial model; the code does not test independence, estimate overdispersion or infer a cause. A production pipeline should version the baseline and defect definition, enforce finalized counts, and show denominator size with every point.

Common Mistakes

  • Comparing percentages while concealing sharply different sample sizes.
  • Recomputing the baseline after every flagged period.
  • Calling a control limit a business target.
  • Treating a signal as proof of the annotated event's effect.

Validation drill

Track 59 weekly inspection proportions with variable sample sizes. Freeze a baseline, flag points beyond their own limits and investigate a week whose rate is high but denominator is small.

title: Asymmetric error bars: tell readers what each endpoint means
summary: Carry lower and upper endpoints with every estimate, and never relabel arbitrary spread as uncertainty.
body:
Carry lower and upper endpoints with every estimate, and never relabel arbitrary spread as uncertainty.

The interval needs a type

An error bar may encode a standard deviation, a confidence interval, a prediction interval, an instrument tolerance or a minimum-to-maximum range. These answer different questions. Put the interval type, level where applicable, method and sample size in the chart caption. Uncertainty displays explain why a narrow-looking interval does not automatically mean a precise individual prediction. A bar without that contract invites the reader to supply the wrong interpretation. If the calculation is model-based, identify the population and conditions under which it applies.

Keep the endpoints, not just a radius

Some intervals are asymmetric around the estimate, especially near natural boundaries or after a nonlinear transform. Export estimate, lower and upper as three separate numbers. A renderer may ask for downward and upward distances, which can be derived from those endpoints without losing meaning. An estimate outside its own stated interval is a data error for many common interval definitions and should be stopped or explained. Forecast fan charts make this distinction even more important because uncertainty often widens with horizon.

Draw limits honestly

If an endpoint falls beyond the plotted axis, do not clip it silently. Extend the axis, use a visible arrow with the endpoint value, or choose another layout. A log axis cannot display zero or negative endpoints; transforming the point and interval requires the same transformation applied to both, with the method stated. Log and symmetric-log scales are not cosmetic switches. The chart should show whether a bound is physical, statistical or merely the display edge.

Compare groups without overclaiming

Overlap of two intervals is not a general significance test, and non-overlap is not the only way to establish a difference. If the decision concerns the difference between groups, estimate and plot that difference with its own interval. Signed differences put zero at the relevant comparison point. Check whether the same subjects appear in both groups; paired data require a paired calculation. For accessible reading, list each estimate and its endpoints in text, with units and the interval definition repeated where the chart may be shared alone.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def errorbar_distances(rows: list[tuple[str, float, float, float]]
                       ) -> list[tuple[str, float, float, float]]:
    names = [name for name, _, _, _ in rows]
    if len(names) != len(set(names)) or any(not name for name in names):
        raise ValueError("estimate labels must be unique and nonempty")
    output = []
    for name, estimate, lower, upper in rows:
        if not all(isfinite(value) for value in (estimate, lower, upper)):
            raise ValueError("estimate and bounds must be finite")
        if not lower <= estimate <= upper:
            raise ValueError("estimate must lie within its interval")
        output.append((name, estimate, estimate - lower, upper - estimate))
    return output

service_intervals = errorbar_distances([
    ("priority queue", 81, 59, 113),
    ("standard queue", 97, 83, 149),
])
assert service_intervals == [
    ("priority queue", 81, 22, 32),
    ("standard queue", 97, 14, 52),
]

Performance and operating cost

Preparing N intervals takes O(N) time and O(N) output space. The code validates geometry but cannot establish that endpoints were calculated with the right statistical method. Keep the original endpoints and method metadata even if the chart library wants only positive distances. Avoid computing an interval from a small sample with an unverified shortcut just because the renderer accepts two numbers.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling a range or standard deviation a confidence interval.
  • Forcing asymmetric endpoints into equal visual arms.
  • Clipping a bound at the axis edge without a marker or label.
  • Inferring a group-difference test only from overlap of separate intervals.

Validation drill

Show 59 response-time estimates with asymmetric intervals. Identify five bounds outside the current axis and revise the view without hiding those endpoints.

title: Q–Q plots: compare distribution shape beyond one summary number
summary: Pair probabilities rather than row positions, state the reference distribution and inspect tail behavior separately.
body:
Pair probabilities rather than row positions, state the reference distribution and inspect tail behavior separately.

A quantile is an ordered position

A Q–Q plot compares quantiles from two distributions at the same cumulative probabilities. It does not pair individual records, even if both samples have the same size. State whether the horizontal axis is an observed reference group or a theoretical distribution, and label units on both axes. ECDF and percentile reading provide the underlying probability view. A line of points near a diagonal suggests broadly similar locations and spreads only if both axes use the same unit and scale; otherwise the reference may have a non-unit slope.

Choose a quantile convention

Software packages differ in how they interpolate between observations. Write down the convention when results will be compared across tools. Repeated values produce repeated or flat stretches; adding random jitter to hide ties changes the apparent pattern. For samples of different sizes, evaluate a common probability grid rather than aligning the first observation of each sorted list. Do not include probability zero or one in a theoretical distribution whose inverse CDF is infinite there. Box and violin views are useful companions when the Q–Q plot is too technical for a general audience.

Read center and tails separately

A nearly straight center with an upward bend in the high tail may indicate more large values in the vertical sample. A shift can move all points above the reference; a scale difference can change the slope. Avoid treating visual departures as an automatic hypothesis test. With a small sample, endpoints are unstable; with a huge sample, slight departures may be practically irrelevant. Sample-size uncertainty belongs in the caption. If the question is about service-level failures, count observations beyond a meaningful threshold as well as inspecting tail curvature.

Keep the comparison reproducible

Filter both samples by the same eligibility and time-window rules, then report their sizes and missing-value counts. If one group contains outages and the other excludes them, the plot is comparing policies as well as distributions. A chart export manifest should include filters, quantile grid, interpolation rule and transformed values. Provide a compact table of selected quantile pairs so a reader can inspect exact numbers without relying on hover or color. Never reverse the axes silently between reports.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def interpolate_quantile(sorted_values: list[float], probability: float) -> float:
    if not sorted_values or not 0 <= probability <= 1:
        raise ValueError("sample and probability are required")
    index = (len(sorted_values) - 1) * probability
    low = int(index)
    high = min(low + 1, len(sorted_values) - 1)
    return sorted_values[low] + (index - low) * (sorted_values[high] - sorted_values[low])

def paired_quantiles(reference: list[float], current: list[float],
                     probabilities: list[float]) -> list[tuple[float, float, float]]:
    if not reference or not current or any(not isfinite(value)
                                            for value in reference + current):
        raise ValueError("samples must contain finite values")
    if any(not 0 <= probability <= 1 for probability in probabilities):
        raise ValueError("probabilities must be inside zero and one")
    first, second = sorted(reference), sorted(current)
    return [(p, interpolate_quantile(first, p), interpolate_quantile(second, p))
            for p in probabilities]

quantile_pairs = paired_quantiles([47, 59, 81, 97, 113],
                                 [52, 61, 83, 101, 129], [0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
assert quantile_pairs == [(0.25, 59, 61), (0.5, 81, 83), (0.75, 97, 101)]

Performance and operating cost

Sorting reference and current samples of sizes A and B takes O(A log A + B log B) time; Q paired probabilities take O(Q) additional time and output space. The code uses linear interpolation at index (N minus one) times probability. It compares two empirical distributions, not a theoretical normal curve or a significance test. Preserve the method and sample sizes with the plot.

Common Mistakes

  • Pairing rows by index instead of pairing equal probabilities.
  • Switching interpolation methods between reports without disclosure.
  • Jittering ties until they look like genuine tail structure.
  • Calling every visible bend a statistically important deviation.

Validation drill

Compare 81 delivery-time records before and after a routing change. Plot common percentiles, report sample counts, and inspect whether the upper tail moved more than the median.

title: Proportional-symbol maps: size circles by area, not radius
summary: Declare the location meaning and value unit, then preserve zero, overlap and boundary context.
body:
Declare the location meaning and value unit, then preserve zero, overlap and boundary context.

A symbol has a location contract

A circle over a map may represent a precise facility, a regional centroid or an approximate address. Those are not equivalent. State what the coordinate means and how much location precision the data support. Choropleth maps color whole regions; proportional symbols encode a value at a point or chosen anchor. Do not place a regional total at a centroid without telling the reader that the circle summarizes an area. If location is sensitive, aggregate or coarsen before publication rather than relying on small marker size to conceal it.

Area should represent quantity

If a symbol encodes a nonnegative count, its visual area should be proportional to that count. Doubling the radius multiplies area by four, exaggerating the larger value. Compute radius from the square root of value relative to a declared maximum. Use a visible reference legend with at least two example magnitudes. A zero count should remain a recorded zero, even if its circle has no area; a tiny outline or table entry may be needed to keep the location discoverable. Scale integrity also means fixing the size domain across maps intended for comparison.

Overlapping circles need an explicit policy

Dense areas can hide smaller symbols under larger ones. Drawing order, opacity and zoom can all change what a reader sees. Try smaller maximum radius, outlines, clustering with disclosed counts, or an alternate ranked table. Do not let overlap remove records from the export. Hexbin density may be better when the question is where point events concentrate, while a proportional-symbol map is better when each point already has a meaningful aggregate. Test overlapping facilities at the closest supported zoom and on a narrow phone viewport.

Count and rate are different maps

A large population center may dominate a count map while having a modest per-person rate. A rate can be mapped with symbol size only if the legend names its denominator and the sampling uncertainty is not buried. Often a count-sized symbol plus a separately encoded rate is too much for one map; use paired maps or a table. The denominator contract must follow the geography and period. Export ID, coordinate meaning, count, denominator, computed rate, symbol radius and suppression state, so the map can be checked without its pixels.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite, sqrt

def area_scaled_radii(values: dict[str, float],
                      maximum_radius: float) -> dict[str, float]:
    if not isfinite(maximum_radius) or maximum_radius <= 0:
        raise ValueError("maximum radius must be positive")
    if not values or any(not place for place in values):
        raise ValueError("locations must be named")
    if any(not isfinite(value) or value < 0 for value in values.values()):
        raise ValueError("mapped values must be finite and nonnegative")
    maximum_value = max(values.values())
    if maximum_value == 0:
        return {place: 0.0 for place in values}
    return {place: maximum_radius * sqrt(value / maximum_value)
            for place, value in values.items()}

service_calls = {"north depot": 47, "south depot": 188, "west depot": 0}
radii = area_scaled_radii(service_calls, 20)
assert radii["south depot"] == 20
assert radii["north depot"] == 10
assert radii["west depot"] == 0

Performance and operating cost

For N locations, finding the maximum and calculating radii takes O(N) time and O(N) output space. The code sizes nonnegative values by area and leaves geographic projection, collision handling and legend generation to the map renderer. A production map must keep one fixed reference maximum across views that readers are expected to compare; recalculating it after every filter changes apparent size.

Common Mistakes

  • Making radius proportional to count and thereby exaggerating area.
  • Treating a regional centroid as an exact event location.
  • Letting large symbols cover small ones without a table or overlap strategy.
  • Comparing maps whose size domains were auto-scaled independently.

Validation drill

Map 59 service depots with zero, small and large call counts. Use area-scaled circles, disclose the location meaning and produce a fixed-size legend for two reporting periods.
