title: Event-aligned charts: choose a baseline before comparing trajectories
summary: Align observations to a real event, retain calendar context and make missing periods explicit.
body:
Align observations to a real event, retain calendar context and make missing periods explicit.

Event time is not calendar time

An event-aligned chart puts each subject's event at relative time zero. This lets a reader compare trajectories before and after events that occurred on different calendar dates. Store the actual event timestamp as well as the relative offset; otherwise seasonality, outages and policy changes disappear. Specify whether an offset means elapsed hours, calendar days or complete reporting periods. Time-series period rules are essential when the event occurs late in a day or across a daylight-saving change.

Fix the baseline rule

A common display subtracts each subject's pre-event value or divides by it. These produce different shapes and units. Select the baseline window before inspecting outcomes, report how many valid observations contributed to it, and reject a percentage change when the baseline is zero. If one subject has only one pre-event measurement and another has 47, their aligned curves carry different reliability. Denominator and grain rules should stay visible with the chart. Plot absolute values alongside normalized values when the magnitude of the original series matters.

Missing is not flat

Do not fill missing pre-event days with the baseline or connect a line across an unobserved outage without a marker. A cohort average at relative day five may use fewer subjects than at day one because follow-up ends; show the contributing count by offset. Attrition can make a trend look like improvement. Small-sample uncertainty belongs near sparse tails, and forecast intervals must not be substituted for missing actual observations.

The line does not prove an effect

A change at time zero can reflect selection into the event, a concurrent intervention, regression to the mean or ordinary seasonality. An annotation identifies timing, not causality. Compare a relevant untreated group or a pre-specified benchmark if the decision requires an effect estimate, and state the assumptions of that comparison. Annotation and causal-claim boundaries apply here. Export subject ID, event date, relative offset, original value, baseline window, normalized value and eligibility state so every plotted line can be reconstructed.

Worked contract

from datetime import date
from math import isfinite

def event_aligned_change(event_day: date, observations: dict[date, float],
                         baseline_days: tuple[date, ...]
                        ) -> list[tuple[int, float, float]]:
    if not baseline_days or len(set(baseline_days)) != len(baseline_days):
        raise ValueError("baseline days must be distinct")
    if any(day >= event_day or day not in observations for day in baseline_days):
        raise ValueError("baseline must be observed before the event")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for value in observations.values()):
        raise ValueError("observations must be finite")
    baseline = sum(observations[day] for day in baseline_days) / len(baseline_days)
    return sorted(((day - event_day).days, value, value - baseline)
                  for day, value in observations.items())

incident_counts = {
    date(2026, 10, 5): 47, date(2026, 10, 6): 59,
    date(2026, 10, 8): 38, date(2026, 10, 9): 35,
}
aligned = event_aligned_change(
    date(2026, 10, 7), incident_counts,
    (date(2026, 10, 5), date(2026, 10, 6)),
)
assert aligned == [(-2, 47, -6), (-1, 59, 6), (1, 38, -15), (2, 35, -18)]
assert all(offset != 0 for offset, _, _ in aligned)

Performance and operating cost

For N observations and B baseline days, validation and averaging take O(N+B) time; sorting relative periods takes O(N log N) time and O(N) output space. The function leaves missing event day zero absent instead of inventing a value. Calendar dates are appropriate only when day-level reporting is the contract; intraday events need zoned timestamps and a declared binning method. Subtracting a baseline describes change, not a causal estimate.

Common Mistakes

  • Discarding calendar dates after alignment and losing concurrent-event context.
  • Choosing a favorable baseline window after seeing the result.
  • Drawing a continuous line over days with no observations.
  • Calling a post-event change proof that the event caused it.

Validation drill

Align 81 facilities around a maintenance intervention. Show each facility's baseline window and post-event coverage, then recompute the cohort curve using only facilities observed through day 14.

title: Interactive charts: make selection work without a pointer
summary: Treat focus, selection and the data table as part of the chart's public interface.
body:
Treat focus, selection and the data table as part of the chart's public interface.

Hover is not access

A tooltip visible only on pointer hover excludes keyboard and many touch users. Give each interactive mark a reachable focus target, a meaningful accessible name and the same detail on focus as on hover. Arrow keys can move within a series, while Home and End can jump to its bounds; publish the key rules next to the chart. Keep a visible focus indicator. Color and text alternatives cover the static layer, but a chart with filters and selections also needs an interaction contract.

Separate focus from selection

Focus says where keyboard input will act. Selection says which records are included in the current analysis. Do not silently change the filter merely because focus moved to another point. If Enter selects a point, announce the new selection and update the related table or summary. A selected range should survive a resize and a redraw by stable record IDs rather than pixel coordinates. Linked filters and cohort state should make the selected population and denominator visible across all charts.

Avoid a thousand tab stops

Putting every mark in the page's normal Tab sequence can make a dense chart unusable. A single chart entry point followed by arrow-key movement may be better, provided the active point's name and value are exposed, the user can exit with Tab, and the navigation order is predictable. Do not trap focus inside the plot. For large series, offer direct search, a bounded table, or a downloadable data file so a user does not have to press an arrow 4,700 times. Large-series reduction must preserve access to underlying records when visual points are aggregated.

The table is a first-class view

An accessible data table should use the same filters, units, missing-value markers and ordering as the chart. If the chart displays a sampled or binned series, identify that fact and provide a route to full records when appropriate. Do not generate a table from SVG positions; derive both views from one data model. Export provenance should include the selection, filter and sort state so a shared screenshot and a CSV tell the same story. Test with only a keyboard, at narrow width, and with zoom before publication.

Worked contract

function nextChartPoint(currentIndex, pointCount, key) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(pointCount) || pointCount < 1 ||
      !Number.isInteger(currentIndex) || currentIndex < 0 ||
      currentIndex >= pointCount) {
    throw new RangeError("chart point state is invalid");
  }
  if (key === "ArrowRight" || key === "ArrowDown") {
    return Math.min(currentIndex + 1, pointCount - 1);
  }
  if (key === "ArrowLeft" || key === "ArrowUp") {
    return Math.max(currentIndex - 1, 0);
  }
  if (key === "Home") return 0;
  if (key === "End") return pointCount - 1;
  return currentIndex;
}

const visibleRecordIds = ["depot-47", "depot-59", "depot-83"];
let focusedIndex = 0;
focusedIndex = nextChartPoint(focusedIndex, visibleRecordIds.length, "End");
if (visibleRecordIds[focusedIndex] !== "depot-83") {
  throw new Error("keyboard focus must follow chart order");
}
if (nextChartPoint(focusedIndex, visibleRecordIds.length, "ArrowRight") !== 2) {
  throw new Error("focus must stop at the last record");
}

Performance and operating cost

A key transition takes O(1) time and space; the displayed order and accessible table require O(N) record storage for N visible points. The pure function handles movement only. The browser component must connect it to focus, accessible names, announcement text and selection state, and must retain Tab exit. If a virtualized chart reorders records, map stable IDs to the new order before restoring focus. Treat the table as the source-aligned view, not as a decorative duplicate.

Common Mistakes

  • Making hover-only tooltip content unavailable on focus and touch.
  • Changing the selected cohort whenever a user merely moves focus.
  • Adding every dense-series mark to the Tab order with no shortcut or data table.
  • Restoring focus by pixel position after filter changes instead of stable record identity.

Validation drill

Audit a 188-point chart using only keyboard navigation. Verify focus visibility, Enter selection, Tab exit, a synchronized table and stable record identity after a filter change.

title: CUSUM charts: accumulate small departures from a stable target
summary: Define the reference process, update rule and alert threshold before reading a rising trace.
body:
Define the reference process, update rule and alert threshold before reading a rising trace.

A cumulative trace needs a frozen baseline

A cumulative-sum chart can detect a sustained small departure that a point-by-point threshold misses. Start with a process metric measured at consistent intervals and a target estimated from an independent, stable baseline period. A cumulative sum of raw values will drift simply because the metric is positive; subtract the target and a reference allowance before accumulating evidence of an upward shift. Use a separate lower trace for downward shifts. P charts handle varying binomial denominators; their rate and limits should not be replaced by a CUSUM of unadjusted percentages. If observation precision or exposure changes across periods, standardize or model that change before applying a fixed CUSUM rule.

The allowance and threshold are design choices

In a tabular upper CUSUM, each new value adds its deviation from the target minus an allowance, and negative running totals reset to zero. A lower CUSUM mirrors the logic for downward movement. The allowance controls the size of shift the chart is tuned to notice; the decision threshold controls when an alert is raised. Neither number is a universal constant. Calibrate them against the operational false-alarm rate and detection delay the team can tolerate, using an appropriate baseline model. Uncertainty displays help explain how noisy short runs can be. The worked numbers below demonstrate mechanics only and must not be copied as an alert policy for another process.

A signal is a review trigger

Mark the exact first threshold crossing on the chart. Keep every earlier point and the zero resets visible; truncating the history can make the signal look instantaneous. An alert says the observed sequence is unusual under the chosen reference model, not that a particular maintenance event caused it. Event annotations need timestamps and a caution about causal interpretation. If a baseline is re-estimated after every signal, the chart can absorb the very drift it was intended to detect. Version the target, allowance, threshold and any planned reset date. When a legitimate process change establishes a new operating state, start a documented new chart rather than silently splicing scales.

Audit the measurement pipeline

A sustained run of delayed, duplicated or missing readings can resemble a process shift. Validate sampling cadence, units, sensor identity and data revision status before interpreting the trace. Time-series gaps must remain gaps or be handled by an explicit rule; inserting zero will push a lower trace down for the wrong reason. Serial correlation also changes the false-alarm behavior of a rule calibrated for independent observations. Keep an export with period ID, raw reading, target version, upper and lower cumulative values, and alert state. Chart manifests make the calculation reproducible after a dashboard or threshold update.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def process_shift_trace(readings: list[float], target: float,
                        allowance: float, threshold: float):
    if (not all(isfinite(value) for value in [*readings, target,
                                               allowance, threshold])
            or allowance < 0 or threshold <= 0):
        raise ValueError("finite readings, nonnegative allowance and positive threshold required")
    upper = lower = 0.0
    trace = []
    for period_index, reading in enumerate(readings, start=1):
        upper = max(0.0, upper + reading - target - allowance)
        lower = max(0.0, lower + target - reading - allowance)
        trace.append((period_index, upper, lower,
                      upper >= threshold, lower >= threshold))
    return trace

depot_trace = process_shift_trace([48, 49, 52, 54],
                                  target=47, allowance=2, threshold=8)
assert depot_trace[:2] == [(1, 0.0, 0.0, False, False),
                           (2, 0.0, 0.0, False, False)]
assert depot_trace[-1] == (4, 8.0, 0.0, True, False)

Performance and operating cost

Updating N readings takes O(N) time and O(N) space when the full trace is retained; an online alarm needs O(1) state. The sequence reaches the illustrative upper threshold only after two larger readings accumulate. No false-alarm guarantee follows from those values. Choose target, allowance and threshold from the real measurement process and validate assumptions such as independence or expected exposure before production alerts.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a target recomputed from the same drifting window being monitored.
  • Copying example allowance and threshold values into a live alert without calibration.
  • Filling missing readings with zero or treating duplicate periods as independent evidence.
  • Calling the first alert proof of a specific cause rather than a trigger for investigation.

Validation drill

Monitor 47 daily throughput readings. Freeze a baseline version, compare an upper and lower trace, record every reset, and test how one missing day changes the alert when it is omitted versus incorrectly filled with zero.

title: Probability calibration plots: compare predicted risk with observed frequency
summary: Build a reliability table with honest bin counts, event rates and a fixed evaluation cohort.
body:
Build a reliability table with honest bin counts, event rates and a fixed evaluation cohort.

Separate ranking from calibrated probability

A score can rank likely events well yet overstate their chance. A calibration plot asks whether cases assigned a given probability experience the event at approximately that frequency. For an equipment-alert model, a group with average predicted failure probability 0.31 should have an observed failure share near 0.31 over a sufficiently large, representative evaluation set. This is not a claim about any single device. Regression overlays often invite a best-fit line; a calibration plot instead compares observed and predicted rates against the identity diagonal. Ranking metrics, decision thresholds and the cost of false alarms answer different questions and should be displayed separately.

Construct bins without concealing support

Partition predictions with a stated rule. Equal-width bins have stable numeric boundaries but may leave some bins thin; equal-count bins balance support yet their boundaries move between cohorts. For each nonempty bin, plot mean predicted probability on x and observed event fraction on y. Include count and event count in a table or label, because a point based on 7 cases is not as stable as one based on 700. Do not join empty bins with a line. The code uses fixed equal-width bins and makes p=1 belong to the final bin. Small-sample displays explain why approximate agreement needs interval context, especially near the extremes.

Protect the evaluation split

Calibration estimated on the same records used to fit or tune a model is optimistic. Hold out an evaluation period or cohort and keep its definition stable. If scores are recalibrated, fit that transformation on a separate calibration set, then evaluate it on untouched data. Log model version, score timestamp, outcome window and censoring or delayed-label policy. A device marked as no failure before its observation window closes is not a verified negative. Provisional periods must be separated from complete labels. Also show prevalence: when base failure rate shifts between cohorts, the curve may move even if the model's ranking stays useful.

Inspect slices and drift carefully

A global curve can hide one badly miscalibrated plant or device family. Compare slices only when each has enough cases, and keep the same bin boundaries and evaluation window. Report omitted records and missing scores. Point movement between months may be sampling noise, model drift or a change in who gets scored; the plot alone cannot distinguish them. Small multiples with shared scales make comparisons less deceptive, while an export manifest keeps model and data versions attached to the image. Provide the underlying bin table so readers can check the plotted rates rather than measuring the diagonal by eye.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def calibration_bins(records: list[tuple[str, float, bool]], width: int = 5):
    if type(width) is not int or width <= 0:
        raise ValueError("bin count must be positive")
    identifiers = [device_id for device_id, _, _ in records]
    if len(identifiers) != len(set(identifiers)) or any(not item for item in identifiers):
        raise ValueError("device IDs must be unique and nonempty")
    bins = [[0, 0.0, 0] for _ in range(width)]
    for _, probability, failed in records:
        if (not isfinite(probability) or not 0 <= probability <= 1
                or type(failed) is not bool):
            raise ValueError("probabilities and event flags must be valid")
        bucket = min(int(probability * width), width - 1)
        bins[bucket][0] += 1
        bins[bucket][1] += probability
        bins[bucket][2] += failed
    return [(bucket, count, score_sum / count, events / count, events)
            for bucket, (count, score_sum, events) in enumerate(bins)
            if count]

inspection_results = [("unit-47", 0.22, False),
                      ("unit-59", 0.31, True),
                      ("unit-83", 0.37, False),
                      ("unit-97", 1.0, True)]
reliability = calibration_bins(inspection_results)
assert reliability[0] == (1, 3, 0.3, 1 / 3, 1)
assert reliability[1] == (4, 1, 1.0, 1.0, 1)

Performance and operating cost

For N predictions and B fixed bins, accumulation takes O(N + B) time and O(B + N) space because unique IDs are validated. Empty bins are omitted rather than invented. The four-record check demonstrates bin assignment and arithmetic, not credible calibration evidence; real evaluation needs sufficient support, a held-out cohort and uncertainty intervals. The function does not estimate those intervals or repair delayed labels.

Common Mistakes

  • Using training records as the final reliability evaluation.
  • Plotting one bin point without its case count or event count.
  • Calling a high-ranking score calibrated without comparing observed frequency.
  • Treating unfinished outcome windows as verified negatives.

Validation drill

Hold out 470 device predictions. Build fixed bins for two months, print counts and event rates, then identify whether a shifted curve also coincides with changed prevalence or incomplete labels.

title: Precision–recall curves: preserve threshold ties and class prevalence
summary: Build an auditable precision–recall staircase from held-out scores, then read average precision against the actual event rate.
body:
Build an auditable precision–recall staircase from held-out scores, then read average precision against the actual event rate.

Start with the decision population

A precision–recall curve describes a ranked binary score across possible alert thresholds. Precision is true alerts divided by all alerts; recall is true alerts divided by all actual events. They answer different questions. If a maintenance team can inspect 47 machines per shift, the useful region may be the high-precision, low-recall end, while a safety review may tolerate many inspections to find nearly every fault. Define the event, prediction timestamp, outcome window, eligible population and positive class before plotting. Probability calibration answers whether a score of 0.30 corresponds to about 30% observed risk; a precision–recall curve asks how selected alerts trade false alarms for captured events. A ranking can be useful and still be poorly calibrated.

Sweep tied scores as one threshold

Sort records by decreasing score. At each distinct score, include all records with that score before measuring precision and recall. Splitting tied cases in arbitrary input order invents operating points that no threshold can achieve. Add a no-alert endpoint at recall zero and precision one only as a plotting convention: it does not mean the model has already found an event. At the opposite end, all eligible records are selected and precision equals the cohort event rate. The stepwise curve must retain its actual points; smoothing or interpolating precision can imply a threshold that never existed. An empirical CDF uses a similar idea of preserving observed steps rather than drawing a continuous story through discrete decisions.

Interpret area and baseline carefully

Average precision weights precision at each achieved recall increment. It is not always the same number as trapezoidal area under a line interpolated between curve points, and neither is classification accuracy. The event prevalence is a useful no-skill reference when scores are independent of labels; if prevalence changes from one plant to another, the apparent precision of the same ranking can change too. Put both event count and total eligible count beside every panel. Compare models on the same untouched evaluation cohort, outcome definition and time window. Shared small-multiple scales stop separate panels from hiding the difficult low-recall region. When costs matter, also show the selected operating threshold and its alert volume rather than publishing only a scalar summary.

Expose uncertainty and selection limits

Few positives produce large stair steps: one additional true event can move recall markedly. Bootstrap or another justified interval method may describe sampling uncertainty, but resample at the correct independent unit, such as machine or customer, when multiple records belong to one unit. Delayed outcomes, unreviewed alerts and selectively labeled negatives can bias the curve; an apparent negative is not a confirmed one merely because a record is old. Small-sample uncertainty and provisional periods need explicit treatment. A companion table should give threshold, true positives, false positives, precision, recall and selected count at a few operationally relevant cuts.

Worked contract

def precision_recall_steps(records: list[tuple[str, float, bool]]):
    from math import isfinite
    identifiers = [record_id for record_id, _, _ in records]
    if len(identifiers) != len(set(identifiers)) or any(not key for key in identifiers):
        raise ValueError("record identifiers must be unique and nonempty")
    if any(not isfinite(score) or type(event) is not bool
           for _, score, event in records):
        raise ValueError("finite scores and boolean labels are required")
    positives = sum(event for _, _, event in records)
    if positives == 0:
        raise ValueError("recall requires at least one positive")
    ranked = sorted(records, key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
    points = []
    true_positives = false_positives = cursor = 0
    while cursor < len(ranked):
        threshold = ranked[cursor][1]
        while cursor < len(ranked) and ranked[cursor][1] == threshold:
            true_positives += ranked[cursor][2]
            false_positives += not ranked[cursor][2]
            cursor += 1
        selected = true_positives + false_positives
        points.append((threshold, true_positives / selected,
                       true_positives / positives, selected))
    average_precision = sum(
        precision * (recall - (points[index - 1][2] if index else 0))
        for index, (_, precision, recall, _) in enumerate(points))
    return points, average_precision, positives / len(records)

inspection_scores = [("press-47", 0.91, True),
                     ("press-59", 0.73, False),
                     ("press-83", 0.73, True),
                     ("press-97", 0.22, False)]
steps, average_precision, prevalence = precision_recall_steps(inspection_scores)
assert len(steps) == 3
assert steps[1] == (0.73, 2 / 3, 1.0, 3)
assert abs(average_precision - 5 / 6) < 1e-12
assert prevalence == 0.5

Performance and operating cost

Sorting N records takes O(N log N) time. The threshold sweep is O(N), while the sorted copy and output need O(N) space; unique-ID validation also needs O(N) space. The sample's average precision is 5/6 because recall rises first by one half at precision one and then by one half at precision two thirds. Four records demonstrate arithmetic and tie handling, not a credible model comparison. The function assumes labels are complete and the evaluation cohort has already been held out.

Common Mistakes

  • Breaking equal scores in row order and presenting unreachable thresholds.
  • Calling trapezoidal interpolation average precision without defining the calculation.
  • Comparing curves built from cohorts with different prevalence or outcome windows.
  • Reading the no-alert plotting endpoint as measured model performance.

Validation drill

Evaluate 470 held-out inspection scores with 59 confirmed events. Print every attainable tied-score threshold, mark the 47-alert operating point, and compare its event capture with the full curve.

title: Autocorrelation plots: align equal-spaced periods before reading lag peaks
summary: Calculate lagged association only over valid pairs, report support by lag and distinguish a seasonal clue from a causal explanation.
body:
Calculate lagged association only over valid pairs, report support by lag and distinguish a seasonal clue from a causal explanation.

A lag must mean the same elapsed time

An autocorrelation plot places lag on the horizontal axis and the association between a series and its own shifted values on the vertical axis. Lag two means two sampling intervals, not merely two available rows. If a daily series skips Tuesday and the values on Monday and Wednesday are adjacent in a database query, treating them as lag one silently changes the elapsed time. Choose a fixed sampling schedule, sort by period, reject duplicates and gaps or apply a separately documented missing-data policy. The simple ledger below requires consecutive integer period IDs and finite measurements. Gap and calendar rules establish the input contract; event-aligned charts answer a different timing question.

Show pair counts, not just spikes

At lag k, only N minus k aligned pairs remain from N complete observations. Large lags therefore have less support, and a dramatic coefficient based on four pairs is fragile. Print the number of pairs beside a selected coefficient or in a companion table. The worked code uses Pearson correlation with means recalculated for each aligned pair set. This is a descriptive lagged Pearson coefficient, not every software package's traditional autocorrelation-function estimator, which may use a full-series mean and normalization. Name the estimator before comparing values across tools. A constant member of a pair set has zero variance, so the coefficient is undefined; display a missing mark instead of a fabricated zero. Small-sample display keeps thin tails visible without overstating them.

Read repetition cautiously

An alternating workload may produce a negative lag-one value and a positive lag-two value. A slow trend can also produce several high positive lag values even without a repeating cycle. A weekly schedule, a changed product mix or an instrumentation reset may create peaks that disappear after appropriate stratification or differencing. Inspect the run chart and known operational calendar before calling a spike seasonality. Correlation at a lag is not evidence that an earlier observation causes a later one. If the goal is forecasting, validate the candidate lag on held-out future periods and avoid using future values while constructing features. Forecast intervals describe predictive uncertainty, while event annotations make causal claims easier to audit.

Treat reference bands as assumptions

A horizontal zero line helps read sign. Statistical confidence bands require a noise model, chosen estimator and a policy for many inspected lags; a generic shaded band is not a universal significance test. Adjacent lag estimates are related, and checking dozens of lags invites chance extremes. Freeze a practical maximum lag based on the question and available pairs, then disclose it. When input values are residuals from a fitted model, describe that fit and its validation window; residual autocorrelation can expose missing structure, but a model trained on the entire evaluation span can hide it. Compare adjacent operational phases on the same vertical scale and keep period count, gap policy and estimator in the export. An export manifest carries the needed calculation details.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite, sqrt

def lagged_pearson(readings: list[tuple[int, float]], max_lag: int):
    if len(readings) < 4 or not 1 <= max_lag <= len(readings) - 3:
        raise ValueError("retain at least three pairs at every requested lag")
    periods = [period for period, _ in readings]
    values = [value for _, value in readings]
    if (any(not isinstance(period, int) for period in periods) or
            any(current != previous + 1
                for previous, current in zip(periods, periods[1:])) or
            any(not isfinite(value) for value in values)):
        raise ValueError("readings must be ordered, consecutive and finite")
    coefficients = []
    for lag in range(1, max_lag + 1):
        before, after = values[:-lag], values[lag:]
        count = len(before)
        before_mean = sum(before) / count
        after_mean = sum(after) / count
        centered_before = [value - before_mean for value in before]
        centered_after = [value - after_mean for value in after]
        numerator = sum(left * right for left, right in zip(centered_before,
                                                            centered_after))
        spread_before = sum(value * value for value in centered_before)
        spread_after = sum(value * value for value in centered_after)
        correlation = (numerator / sqrt(spread_before * spread_after)
                       if spread_before and spread_after else None)
        coefficients.append((lag, count, correlation))
    return coefficients

alternating_load = list(zip(range(47, 55), [47.0, 59.0] * 4))
lag_summary = lagged_pearson(alternating_load, 3)
assert lag_summary[0] == (1, 7, -1.0)
assert lag_summary[1] == (2, 6, 1.0)
assert lag_summary[2] == (3, 5, -1.0)
assert lagged_pearson([(47, 83.0), (48, 83.0), (49, 83.0),
                       (50, 83.0)], 1)[0][2] is None

Performance and operating cost

For N readings and K requested lags, each lag builds and scans N minus k paired values, yielding O(N·K) time and O(N + K) extra space, including temporary centered lists and the result. This favors an inspectable short-lag audit over an optimized transform; large K and long series justify a separately tested faster estimator with its own normalization rules. The eight-period alternating example returns minus one at lags one and three, plus one at lag two, and support counts seven, six and five. Constant readings return an undefined coefficient rather than a false zero.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating consecutive database rows as consecutive time periods after a gap.
  • Comparing coefficients from different estimator conventions without naming the method.
  • Calling a high-lag spike seasonality when only a handful of pairs remain.
  • Adding generic significance bands without a noise model or multiple-lag policy.

Validation drill

Take 83 completed daily workload measurements. Audit dates for gaps and duplicates, predeclare seven lags, plot each lagged coefficient with its pair count, then compare the result with a run chart and the known weekly operating schedule.

title: Seasonal subseries plots: compare the same cycle position across years
summary: Group repeated cycle positions, draw their chronological traces and calculate reference means only from complete cycles.
body:
Group repeated cycle positions, draw their chronological traces and calculate reference means only from complete cycles.

Choose a cycle for a real operational reason

A seasonal subseries plot groups observations by their position within a known repeating cycle: all first quarters together, all second quarters together and so on. Within each group, preserve chronological order across cycles and draw a reference mean or median for that position. The view exposes both differences between cycle positions and changes within one position over years. A quarterly series needs four positions; a weekly schedule might need seven weekdays. Do not infer the cycle merely because a pattern looks attractive after trying many candidates. Document the calendar origin and whether a period is a full business day, fiscal week or standard month. Autocorrelation plots can suggest repetition, but their lag peaks do not supply the business calendar. Time-series calendar rules fix the period definitions.

Align like positions and keep the trend visible

A quarter-one rise across years can coexist with quarter three being the seasonal high. If the group means are calculated over the entire time span, a rising long-term trend can make later years look elevated at every position and exaggerate a seasonal story. Inspect the original chronological series and, when justified, a separately labeled detrended view. Do not quietly subtract a trend and publish the adjusted trace as raw volume. The seasonal subseries plot is descriptive; a repeated peak does not establish that the calendar position causes it. Keep all panels on one vertical scale so a small within-quarter change is not magnified by a custom axis. Shared-scale panels and event annotations make context visible without overclaiming.

Do not let an unfinished cycle define the reference

A current year with only two complete quarters can contribute those two observed points, but it must not be treated as a four-quarter baseline. Mark its unobserved quarters as missing, not zero, and freeze the complete historical cycles used for the reference means. A backfilled quarter can change the baseline; version that change. The code below requires each reference cycle to contain every position once and permits a later incomplete cycle for display only. Real calendar data also need an explicit policy for holidays, leap days, 53-week years and corrected reports. Counts behind averages belong in the accompanying table. Calendar completeness and missing-cell encoding apply when the same data is shown as a matrix.

Make the grouped view answer a concrete question

For capacity planning, ask whether the same quarter reliably peaks, whether peak magnitude is changing and whether the latest complete point is unusual relative to its own season. A grouped trace can reveal that a conventional time-series line obscures those comparisons. Yet two historical cycles are weak evidence of recurrence; unusual one-off events can dominate a group mean. Show the exact number of complete cycles, use a median reference when outliers are common and inspect sensitivity to leaving out a cycle. Do not project the group mean forward as a forecast without an evaluated model and uncertainty. Forecast fan charts have that different purpose. Provide labels and a reference table for readers who cannot distinguish traces by color alone; accessible chart guidance covers the contract.

Worked contract

from collections import defaultdict
from math import isfinite

def seasonal_subseries(readings: list[tuple[int, int, float]],
                       positions: int, last_reference_cycle: int):
    if positions < 2 or not isinstance(last_reference_cycle, int):
        raise ValueError("declare cycle length and reference cutoff")
    by_position = defaultdict(list)
    seen = set()
    reference_cycles = set()
    for cycle, position, volume in readings:
        if (not isinstance(cycle, int) or not isinstance(position, int) or
                not 1 <= position <= positions or not isfinite(volume) or
                (cycle, position) in seen):
            raise ValueError("cycle positions must be unique, valid and finite")
        seen.add((cycle, position))
        by_position[position].append((cycle, volume))
        if cycle <= last_reference_cycle:
            reference_cycles.add(cycle)
    if not reference_cycles or any(
            (cycle, position) not in seen
            for cycle in reference_cycles for position in range(1, positions + 1)):
        raise ValueError("every reference cycle must be complete")
    result = []
    for position in range(1, positions + 1):
        trace = sorted(by_position[position])
        reference = [volume for cycle, volume in trace
                     if cycle in reference_cycles]
        result.append((position, len(reference), sum(reference) / len(reference), trace))
    return result

quarterly_orders = [(47, 1, 47), (47, 2, 59), (47, 3, 83), (47, 4, 71),
                    (48, 1, 59), (48, 2, 71), (48, 3, 97), (48, 4, 83),
                    (49, 1, 61), (49, 2, 73)]
panels = seasonal_subseries(quarterly_orders, positions=4,
                            last_reference_cycle=48)
assert panels[0] == (1, 2, 53.0, [(47, 47), (48, 59), (49, 61)])
assert panels[2] == (3, 2, 90.0, [(47, 83), (48, 97)])
assert panels[3][3] == [(47, 71), (48, 83)]

Performance and operating cost

For N readings, validation and grouping take O(N) expected time; sorting each position's trace costs O(sum nₛ log nₛ), bounded by O(N log N). Checking reference completeness takes O(C·S) for C reference cycles and S positions. Stored traces and the duplicate-key set need O(N) space. The toy quarterly ledger uses two complete reference years, giving a first-quarter mean of 53 orders and a third-quarter mean of 90. The partial third year appears only where observed, and never changes the frozen reference. Two cycles verify code behavior but cannot establish dependable seasonality.

Common Mistakes

  • Starting the four-position cycle at the wrong fiscal quarter.
  • Treating an unobserved current-quarter cell as a measured zero.
  • Mixing a trend-adjusted trace with raw-volume reference means without labeling the change.
  • Calling a cycle-position mean a validated forecast or causal explanation.

Validation drill

Take 47 completed fiscal years with four quarters each and one partial current year. Audit duplicate and missing quarter keys, show chronological traces for each quarter, calculate references only from complete years, and compare the grouped view with the ungrouped time series.
